utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we have considered your request for further time. Having regard to the evidence which the witness has given and the amount of time which we think you should have available for cross-examination, we'll give you an hour this morning, which is some extra time, although not a great deal. So you have one hour from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, yesterday you said that it was not true, or rather, that what you said was not correct, what you said and published by Pobjeda, the Pobjeda newspaper on the 3rd of October, 1991. I have here - I received this this morning - a photocopy of the issue of Pobjeda, dated the 3rd of October, and I'll hand it in once I receive the original of that issue of the 3rd of October by post. But there's a large photograph in the article. It was taken on the 2nd or 3rd. And it says, "The commemoration paid to the heroes who were killed," and you can see this commemorative meeting taking place on the photograph. And this is what it says in the article, the passage where you yourself are quoted. So I'd like to hear your comments and answer my questions later on: "Nikola Samardzic," it says, "the Foreign Minister, in his speech spoke about the expectations of the forthcoming Hague conference. He spoke of the previous conference and Samardzic reminded us that the Montenegrin delegation had assumed as far as was possible a flexible in order to arrive at a settlement for the Yugoslav crisis and the cease of hostilities. However, the events that took place along the border towards Croatia, and especially what has taken place at the Ravno-Slano line today shows that our casualties of our units were perpetrated on territory that did not belong to Croatia and that the MUP from Croatia had come and attacked our units from an ambush. All this testifies to the fact that Montenegro was attacked by the Croatian MUP and that this was done on purpose. It was an attack, in fact, on the JNA, and Montenegrin guys who were doing their best to serve the JNA." And so on and so forth. I don't want to take up more time with reading out the whole article. Then we also have a quotation by you which was highlighted in the middle of the article, as particularly important, where you say: "I think that the meeting at The Hague will be fairly difficult on the 5th, and I presented this fact because the foreign media are well organised against us. And yesterday, in Dubrovnik, observers demonstrated how Dubrovnik had been attacked by the army and Montenegro at the same time our young men were being killed in Herzegovina. Perhaps this language is somewhat different, but the object is to show that we are being attacked and that we are performing our duty and standing up in defence of our country. "With the issue of Prevlaka, we have to keep proving that Prevlaka is part of our territory, that is to say, is part of Montenegro, and that it was never Croatia. So what right do they now have to take this and attack it? I am experiencing all this as a great tragedy and as being very unfortunate. As things are as they stand, we have to go ahead and fight and defend ourselves. Nikola Samardzic." So yesterday I read out a quotation, and today I read out another quotation. This was a statement given from the report and minutes of a meeting. You questioned that, denied you had ever said it, denied you had ever said that Prevlaka was never Croatian, that it was always -- that it always belonged to Montenegro, whereas this is what the newspapers in 1991 said. So tell me now, please, Mr. Samardzic, why is it that you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Milosevic, you can't go on in this way, talking all the time. Let the witness see the publication which you have. He should have the chance to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've cut the microphone off. Let the witness see it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The article was printed as it stands, the top half and then the bottom half. The photocopy machine only takes an A-4 format, so I had to copy it in that way. But I will be getting the newspapers, the original issue and edition, so I don't think that will be a problem. Mr. May, so as not to waste time, I think that this is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, give me a chance to read through what you've just given me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I read it all out to you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't read it out properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, come on. Let's give it to the interpreters to read, then.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The newspaper Pobjeda quite obviously published what I said, but not what I really said. At that time, the editor of Pobjeda was a man named Konatar, a ultranationalist, who was famed for writings of all kind, articles of all kind in Pobjeda, and the newspaper was even called Konatar's newspaper Pobjeda. He seems to have planted this on me and alleges that I said that, especially that Prevlaka belonged to Montenegro. That's not correct, because everybody else I said that Prevlaka was part of Croatian territory but that we should win it in negotiations with Croatia. That is what I said. And what Milosevic is trying to supplant is just not true, and Konatar as well. This was all within the frameworks of the policy that was waged at the time, in which everybody could say what they wanted as they saw it. So Mr. Milosevic, this means absolutely nothing. The newspaper Pobjeda wrote all sorts of things at that time, and I stand by the fact that I always stated things publicly and said that at that time I acted as I did. I should like to repeat that prior to that and after that, I always claimed that we could win Prevlaka over only in negotiations with Croatia. And secondly, I don't understand what you wish to prove with this article. What is it? What do you want to show?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What it's being produced for is to contradict your evidence. What the accused says is that this is what you were saying at the time, and it, of course, is different to what you're saying now. That's the point, so you understand it. Now, do I understand this to be your position: That the paper has misquoted what you said at that meeting? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely so. That's quite right, Your Honour. The newspaper did not print what I actually said, and at that time, I spoke in the Assembly and at the government session that was held and always said publicly that we should win Prevlaka over in negotiations with Croatia. That is the well-known stance that I took. And this small trick that is being tried here doesn't mean a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Samardzic, is Pobjeda, or was Pobjeda the leading state newspaper of Montenegro at that time? And I'm talking about 1991. Let's say in 1991.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, Pobjeda was in the hands of the ultranationalists, who advocated fighting and aggression to take over Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us deal with this. Is there any further question you want to ask about the article? Because if so, the usher should be able to sit down and the Prosecution can have a look at it. Is there anything else you want to ask about the actual article?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to ask whether Pobjeda was the leading Montenegrin daily at that time, and it still is, I believe, the principal newspaper and official newspaper of the Republic of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the main newspaper in Montenegro, but that does not prove that I actually said those words. I never authorised the article. I never authorised what he wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, you know that all important government sessions and meetings of the Presidency are attended by journalists. They are not closed to the gentlemen of the press. The newspapers report on them. So you were -- this was a leading, official Montenegrin paper, and it is quoting the Foreign Minister of Montenegro. Now you're claiming that they were misquoting you. Did you ever deny what Pobjeda had printed? If you were so flagrantly misquoted, as you now claim, did you ever deny having said that? You were the minister and Pobjeda was the paper.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The truth is that I did not deny it, and at the time I did not have the time to do so, nor was the situation such that I could enter into a quarrel of any kind or take issue with the publication. There are other points made here that I don't understand. You say that this appeared on the 3rd of October. Yesterday you claimed that on the 1st of October the commemorative meeting was held. So you can't have the meeting held on the 1st of October with Pobjeda reporting on it only on the 3rd of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There is no date on that particular copy because it is a copy. But I will get the newspaper, and you'll see that everybody is standing up in the -- to observe the commemorative meeting, and that's what the article is about. It speaks about that commemorative meeting. But let's not waste time there. Mr. Samardzic, I have another question for you now, and it's this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you're moving on to something else, then --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just for a moment --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- this photocopy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... and then we'll make a decision about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I will be producing, once I receive it through the post, the original issue and copy of the newspaper, so that you can see that it is authentic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was not present according with this photo here. This commemoration. [Interpretation] Quite certainly, this is a forgery, and there's been some mix-up, because I can't see myself on the picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he's finished.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Twelve years have elapsed since the meeting, so I have to do my best to recall those days. Your questions are very fast. I can see the photograph. It is a photograph I don't recognise. I wasn't at that meeting and I know that I was -- did not attend any commemorative meeting held in the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right, Mr. Samardzic. As it's a forgery in the newspapers, in 1991, when you were a minister, you can just stand by that claim. I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the Prosecution have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't bother me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, do you know the name Zoran Kovacevic, a captain from the 7th Battalion, perhaps, at that time, of the JNA? Zoran Kovacevic is the name. Do you know him from the days of the conflicts that took place along the Montenegrin-Croatian border and that tripod of Montenegro, Croatia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know any Zoran Kovacevic, and as you're asking me now, I can't link it up with anything. I don't know what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then comment this, please, his statement, and this is today's issue of Pobjeda. It is his statement here that I have, and he was a witness to the events that you're testifying about. I'm going to skip over certain portions where he says that everybody was absolutely revolted, but he said that: "Zoran Kovacevic, captain of the 7th Battalion, came to our offices and says that Samardzic asked him and his fellow fighters to steal on the Dubrovnik theatre of war. 'Samardzic came up to us in front of the Plaza Hotel in the town of Herceg-Novi while we were washing our hands, washing the blood off our hands from our injured comrade. We didn't know who he was, but when he introduced himself as the Foreign Minister, we accepted his invitation to have a drink with him. All our talks about politics and what was going on at the Dubrovnik battlefront, he said, Well, Dubrovnik is going to be ours. There will be happy days for us.' The captain of the 7th Battalion also recounted that Samardzic told them that they had to go back to Debeli Brijeg and The Hague witness today, the Foreign Minister of Montenegro at the time, asked them that if they could, he would appreciate to have a little camper sent to him and that he would give them 300 Deutschmarks in return. 'In other words, Samardzic asked us to steal for him, and he even suggested that we could do the job in the town of Slano, where he said there were a lot of campers that holiday makers used. And he asked that the camper be as big and as long as possible. We were absolutely astounded. We couldn't believe that he was actually asking us to do something like that. And this coming from the Foreign Minister of Montenegro.' And a message to The Hague witness from Captain Kovacevic: "I am not a thief, and that is why I did not want to have the army lose face. That is why I didn't fulfil your expectations, and I'm very sorry that you were left without this big and long trailer, camper.' That is what Captain Kovacevic has to say. And he also adds and says that Nikola Samardzic told him --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is quite impossible for the witness to follow all of this. The witness must have a chance -- he must have a chance to answer you making these allegations. Do you know anything about this, Mr. Samardzic, this Captain Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, first and foremost, I don't know that man. I never saw him in my life. This is nonsense, and it's lies, organised lies, that are intended to disqualify me, discredit me as a witness. And they are being forged in Podgorica today, and there is no trace of the truth. I never asked for a trailer. I could have bought one many times in my life. I didn't need to steal one from the Dubrovnik front line. So this is an absolute pure trick and lie. What they resort to is something that I'm astounded by, also by the volume of lies that the accused Milosevic is presenting against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you that all of Montenegro is astonished --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Remember you're in a court, please, and here he is "Mr. Milosevic." Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He claims that you particularly said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're reading out from a statement. Is this some statement which has been supplied to you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just finish, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you a question. Would you kindly answer. Is this a statement? We ought to know what it is that you've got. Is this a statement which has been supplied to you or is it some other document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give this to you immediately, gentlemen. I just want to ask the witness whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is it a statement -- it's a very simple question: Is it a statement which has been provided to you? Is that what it is?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, this was published in this morning's newspaper in Podgorica, and it's not a statement that was made to me; it was addressed to the entire public, if you read the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is the answer to the question that I was asking you: Yes, it was in the newspaper this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, please, this is nothing that I got. It's not a statement that I got. This is from the newspapers. Did you talk about the house of Tereza Kesovija, the well-known Croat pop singer? And you said that the house was more than rich and there were plenty of things that could be taken from there.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, why are you saying all these crazy things? You are fantasising. Today, Pobjeda is in the hands of Chetniks and they write this way. They are writing this way because they want to smear the name of people from that time, of honest people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But here is a reaction of a man you mentioned here. I personally don't recall his name, but he watched you on television. You mentioned him, and he says, "Samardzic either cannot control himself or has been paid to lie." And this is what he says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's of no use. That's of no use to us. The comment of somebody reprinted in a newspaper about the evidence is of no assistance to the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the man accused by Mr. Samardzic here is reacting, through the newspaper, to these false accusations. I'm asking Mr. Samardzic what he's been doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... to give evidence in due course, if you want, but merely writing something in a newspaper isn't evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. This is the reaction of Predrag Popovic, who you mentioned as some participant from the People's Party, a nationalist, whatever. Mr. Samardzic, what is your reaction to the following: The fact that the Association of Veterans of Montenegro published this. It's right here on the same page of this morning's paper. Today is the 10th. This is again the Pobjeda newspaper that is published in Podgorica, and it says: "The Association expresses its sorrow and its shame before the public that the testimony of Mr. Samardzic is primarily based on --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop this. The opinion of the veterans is neither here nor there. It is of no assistance to this Court. Now, you can put, as you did, an allegation that this witness was involved, as you allege, in the looting. You can put that if you have allegations of that sort to put, but mere comments and abuse is of no assistance to us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I'm just quoting today's newspaper that is published in the capital of Montenegro. That is the principal newspaper there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know our opinion about those matters and whether such questions are admissible. They are only admissible if they are allegations which ought to be put, allegations of alleged fact.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let's move on. Let's try to be as effective as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, what was the number of employees at the foreign ministry of Montenegro when you were minister?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact number. I guess it was about 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So your ministry had a total of 15 employees?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess so. I can't remember the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that you personally did not take part in drafting these questions for Momir Bulatovic, and you were a member of the delegation when that delegation, headed by Momir Bulatovic, went to the United States; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the delegation, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you, as minister accompanying his president, and you head a ministry of a total of 15 employees, have nothing to do with this paper provided by the Foreign Ministry. Do you consider that to be probable, credible to anyone?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because at the same time I was director, manager, of Jugooceanija, and I spent most of my time in Kotor, not Titograd, and I only came to the ministry when there was something urgent going on. So I was not a paid minister. It is quite possible that somebody at the ministry wrote that while I was in Kotor, just before we left. So there's nothing more to it. These are primarily things that you are trying to bring forth in a deceitful manner. I wrote many times about President Wilson, and this could have been used for writing a pro memoria for President Bulatovic. I don't see anything bad about that except for this trick, trying to say that I said that what was going on in Croatia at that time was genocide. So that is really up to Bulatovic and the employee concerned. But I am truly astounded by what Pobjeda wrote this morning. These are such terrible deceits, like what they wrote about Tereza Kesovija. Whoever knows me in Montenegro will understand, and it will be quite clear to them, how great these lies published by Pobjeda this morning are. It is quite impossible that I said any of these things, that I encountered this man, and that any of that happened. In all these tricks and lies, I am truly astonished, but thank God --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why are you going back to that question? We've already dealt with that. I see that you are truly affected by it, upset by it.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to cut the microphone for a moment. Now, don't both speak at the same time. Now, Mr. Milosevic, I think we've gone over this very fully, so perhaps move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you claim that out of this total number of 15 employees you did not know who did what, you were on the delegation with Bulatovic, and somebody else from the ministry, then, prepared these possible questions and answers for him. Who could have done that, Mr. Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not going to go into all of that, but I do know that sometimes when I was in Kotor, that Bulatovic would call in one of my employees to write something for him. That happened not once, but several times. So there is nothing awful about this. And why are you trying to compromise me in this way? This kind of thing actually happened. I remember how things were done at the ministry. When I was not there, and I was not there often because also director of Jugooceanija, then President Bulatovic would call someone from the ministry, an employee, to write something for him. So this could have easily taken place then as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Samardzic. But these documents that I've presented to you - there are several documents - some you could not deny, and I see that you're denying this one, this speaks of the political and diplomatic position of the government and its activities, that you were a member of. So that includes you too. Isn't that quite clear -- isn't it quite clear that you are saying something quite different today, 11 years later?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not contrary at all. I have proven this before the Court, and I have original notes from the meetings of the Assembly. And what I advocated in Vienna and also on the 17th and 18th of October, when I said clearly that I condemn the policy that you pursued then, both in Serbia and in Montenegro and towards Croatia. I condemned it. So you cannot deceive anyone here by saying that that's what I did. There are many documents from that period. I could also put questions to you: What is this? What is that? Where do you get all these things that you're trying to trick me with? You are trying to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, the accused is entitled to ask his questions, and try and answer them, if you would, as shortly as possible. Now, Mr. Milosevic, in your part, don't repeat questions which you've asked before.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no intention of repeating them. All of this is quite sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Samardzic, on page 15, towards the end of the second paragraph - I'm speaking about your statement now, the 30-page statement or whatever the number of pages - you speak about your decision to resign from your post as Foreign Minister, and then you say that you were prevented from doing so by Hrvoje Kacic, a Croatian official and your friend, chairman of the foreign policy committee of the parliament of Croatia. You acted on his suggestions, as you explained this now; you did not resign. From then on, you represented the interests of Croatia and the government of Montenegro. Is that correct, Mr. Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is an absolute lie. This is deceitful. I never represented the interests of Croatia and the government of Montenegro. I represented the interests of the Montenegrin people in this grave tragedy that was taking place then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Samardzic. Very well. Tell me, please: Give me an answer to the following question. I have to deal with quite a few areas now, because I see that time is running out. Why are you untruthfully representing the role of the Serbian Orthodox church and Amfilohije Radovic, the archbishop of Montenegro? On page 22 of your statement, you slandered the church. You said that they were proponents of hatred, killing, and all kinds of crimes. At the same time, you did not offer any proof of that. Of course, that doesn't surprise me that you've offered no proof, because it is a well-known thing that high --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't comment. Don't comment. Just ask a question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you give me any proof for such accusations levelled at the Serbian Orthodox church and Amfilohije Radovic, the archbishop of Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not exactly the way I had put it, the way you read it out. I did mention in the statements two years back, I did mention Amfilohije Radovic, and I repeat today that Amfilohije Radovic, who is head of the Serbian Orthodox church in Montenegro, is a proponent of hatred towards anyone who is not a Serb. That is true. During the war at the Dubrovnik front line, he went there instead of carrying out his duty as a man of the cloth. He was chanting combat songs there, encouraging the army to fight. And his newspaper - Svetigora, I think is the name of the newspaper - during those days, incited hatred and a further struggle with Croatia. It is sufficient to look at his newspaper from those days and to conclude who Amfilohije Radovic is. That does not mean that I have accused all the clergymen of the Serbian Orthodox church. I mentioned Amfilohije Radovic there and I had him in mind primarily. Very many people in Montenegro consider him to be exactly the kind of person that I've described just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a bit more complex than that. This is what it says in your statement: "The anti-Catholic nature of the Dubrovnik offensive should not be underestimated. Both Bulatovic and Djukanovic were violent anti-Catholics, like all pro-Serb extremists were. This position was articulated in the official media, notably by the Serbian Orthodox church." And it is only then that you say the archbishop of the Serbian Orthodox church in Montenegro, Amfilohije Radovic, was professing the most horrible hatred. He also spoke in favour of torturing Croats, and then Muslims later. You are saying that, that he instigated people to kill and torture Croats and Muslims and he personally sang, chanted, along with the gusle, about the glory of Serbia and Montenegro. As a Montenegrin, Mr. Samardzic, I'm sure you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness should have the chance to deal with the passage which has been referred to in the statement. Is there anything you want to say about that, Mr. Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there is something I want to say. I don't think that he is properly reading my statement, if he is actually reading, and then that's not what I said. I condemned Amfilohije then. I mean, I condemned his behaviour. I did not agree with that kind of behaviour, especially not for someone who is supposed to be God's shepherd in Montenegro. And that is the point of the criticism that I raised. I said that he participated in the war at the front line with his gusle, and I don't think that that is proper for a man of the cloth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also talked about instigating killings and torture.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, again they tricked you into giving this kind of statement. Did they plant that into your statement, so your statement is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My statement is correct. What I said now is what I meant, and that's what I said, and I condemn the behaviour of Amfilohije in those days. If that is not sufficient, I really don't know what you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Everything that you have been saying is quite sufficient for me, Mr. Samardzic. I was quoting your statement; I wasn't claiming anything myself. And then on page 22, you go on to say that "Amfilohije, who strove for killings, both in his sermons as well as in his publications ..." So he spoke out in favour of killings, that's what you said. You accuse him of doing this. And your proof is that he was chanting epic poems to the accompaniment of the gusle instrument. That is what every Montenegrin does, old and young. They all sing songs accompanied by the gusle.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they do, but not a church dignitary. He doesn't follow an army, singing to the tune of the gusle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Samardzic. I have understood you -- I always understood that the church was with the people, so that it follows the people where they go. And you said that Branko Kostic went to see the people who had been victims and casualties in attacks and you criticise him for doing that. And you criticise Amfilohije Radovic for going to visit his flock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No need to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You furthermore explain that your positions were very quickly contrary to those held by Bulatovic and Djukanovic, because, as you yourself state, Djukanovic's interests were geared towards Russia, Greece, and the former Soviet republics, whereas you preferred contacts with the West, and that is why you tried to persuade him to change his views. Is that another pure fabrication on your part? It says so on page 5 of your statement. So perhaps you're going to deny it once again and say that your statement is not correct. You are between a rock and a hard place. You don't know what to do. You don't want to say anything against the opposite side and yet you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer. Now, it's been put to you that in your statement you say - and I haven't found it yet --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Page 6. Thank you. It's been put that there was a difference between you and Bulatovic about orientation to other countries. Is there anything you want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how it was written, along those lines, as far as I recall, two years ago. But I want to stress that what I stated here and not two years ago, that is what is relevant. But if he wants me to talk about that and if he's asking me about that, the truth is that in my work at the ministry at that time, the first trips we had was to the East, and I don't think it was a terrible thing if I advised the president, which I suppose I did, that we should orient ourselves towards the West. I made no accusations, because I think that we should cooperate both with the East and with the West. And at that time, Montenegro needed to turn towards the West more than it did towards the East. And we did have meetings in Russia and Kazakhstan and all that was quite in order, quite fine. So I don't see why you're trying to trip me up and why you're saying something quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, I think that you're trying to trip yourself up. All I'm doing is asking you to explain your statement, because you say on page 5, the penultimate paragraph: "I tried to prevail upon Djukanovic to go to Western Europe, Great Britain, France, Germany, and the United States. But he had no desire to go to these places and was actually quite contemptuous of them."

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that. Whatever is written there, I did not put it that way. I am presenting here before the Tribunal matters as I recall them. Now, if this was put into my mouth, I don't think that is in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well, Mr. Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, I presented what we did, how we worked in the ministry, and I don't see that I can be accused of anything. I do not accuse Djukanovic of anything, nor should this be discussed here and now. We are discussing your crimes here and not how the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Montenegro functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, I'm going to ask you whatever I feel like asking you, and not what you want me to ask you, of course within the limitations put on me here. And I am sorry that you cannot get out of the well you've fallen into, the pit you've fallen into, but you can scratch along its walls. You won't be able to get out of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, is there any more cross-examination which is proper?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Mr. May. I do have quite a few more questions. I don't think I'll have time to ask them all, so I'd like to ask you to extend my time, if you would. I don't think I'll get through all my questions in the ten minutes I have left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, although your speech denies you - and I showed the October speech to you - you explained that there was no reason for concern on the part of Montenegro with respect to any aspirations on the part of Croatia, and that Croatia's conduct in that regard was quite civilised, without any territorial pretensions. Now I'm asking you this: Do you recall - and you were minister at that time - do you recall, for example, that on the 23rd of January, 1991, in Zagreb, a meeting was held of the representatives of Croatia and Montenegro? So the date is the 23rd of January, 1991. At that meeting, the then president of the Croatian Sabor or parliament, Zarko Domljan, stated that Croatia considers the area of Boka Kotorska, the Bay of Kotor, to be its own territory, and the Assembly of Montenegro and the whole Yugoslav public was informed of this through the debate that was held at the Montenegrin parliamentary debate on February of that same year. And it was televised directly via Television Montenegro, so this was no propaganda. It was publicly stated, and many times asserted facts and direct coverage from the meetings and sessions of the Montenegrin Assembly. Do you remember that, and do you consider that to be worrying for Montenegro, that it gave rise for concern? And do you consider it justified for it to defend that territory that belonged to it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that at all, and once again, I think that you have made a forgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. You don't remember. Let me go on. We haven't got time. You say you don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him finish. You've put something to him. Let him finish.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend that meeting in Zagreb, the one you claim to have taken place, nor can I remember that anybody in Croatia put it that way, said that. Now, you can bring in newspapers, like Konatar's newspaper or today's Pobjeda issue, or whatever you like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, you must let the accused ask the questions and give him time. Just restrict your answers, if you would, to dealing with the questions. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. You've got slightly over ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear you. How much more? Ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Slightly over ten minutes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means until 20 to 11.00; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not the clock I'm looking at. It means 25 to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Perhaps you're looking at it from a different angle of vision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, let me ask you this, something that you uttered into the microphone and not something you wrote into your statement. You said that in Montenegro, a nationalist putsch had been effected, which brought Djukanovic and Bulatovic into power, or rather, Bulatovic and Djukanovic, in that order. Is that what you said? Is that what you uttered into this microphone here?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that a nationalistic putsch did take place. I don't recall having mentioned Bulatovic and Djukanovic in that context, because they didn't come into power straight away. They were elected at the end of the year. The putsch took place at the beginning of the year and they were elected at the end of the year, after the elections. That is what I said, and you're trying to trip me up again. So I'm not here either to attack Djukanovic or Bulatovic, but you seem to be going round and round in circles and trying to trip me up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you what I feel like asking you, what I want to ask. Tell me, then: Who took over power in Montenegro with the advent of that nationalist putsch?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I took over power and authority in Montenegro; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So who was at the head of Montenegro at that time in my name, on my behalf? Because I wasn't there. So please tell me: Who executed power in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a certain group of people acting in your name. And the group that came in power was working for you. Then Milo Djukanovic turned this about and changed the power and authority. He did that for a full five years. And you keep saying that I'm attacking Milo Djukanovic; because he stands in opposition to you, I'm not going to attack him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, I'm not linking you with any attacks on Milo Djukanovic. All I'm doing is asking you something. And as you said that he was against me, I don't need to defend him. I have no reason to defend him. I'm just defending the truth, and what you're saying here is untruths. You have written 30 pages here against him and against his brother, accusing him and his brother, and of course I feel duty-bound to defend the truth.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not write anything against him or his brother. What was written about his brother I said was a mistake, an error, and that I said that Jezda the boss knew about the weapons, not him. You tried to trip me up and you're doing it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Whether -- I don't try to trip anybody up. But would you tell me through whom it was that I was managing Montenegro when the nationalistic putsch took place?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the people who had effected the putsch; the army and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please, what did the army and the police have to do in the demonstration that took place in Montenegro? Not a single flower was trampled on. Not a single window was shattered, so what does the army and the police have to do with it? What are you talking about, Mr. Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody did say that any windows were shattered or flowers trampled on. The army was there under your control and the police was there under your control, and they had taken over power and authority, so it is quite certain that you were the initiator of what took place in Montenegro, the so-called Anti-Bureaucratic revolution. That is your act. And I stand by that. What more do you want?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who, then, assumed power in Montenegro except me? Because you say I did. I don't know that I was in power in Montenegro, but if you say so, if you claim so, well, then. So tell me now: Who was in power in my name?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the elections, it was Milo and Momir. What more do you want?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, just wait a minute. Aren't you contradicting yourself? Were they legally elected at the topmost party elections in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what's the putsch you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The putsch took place before that. They wouldn't have come to power had there not been the putsch, and that is quite certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ah, so the people would not have voted for them had the putsch not taken place; is that it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those are your conclusions. Let's leave that, whether they would or would not vote. Up until then, they were not people that held such high functions, high offices. They were not in the top echelons of power. And at the time, they were people who you trusted, and that is nothing terrible. This is common knowledge in Montenegro. You yourself are aware of it and know it full well. And Milo Djukanovic came to realise the policy you were implementing and turned against you, and you can't make me attack him here today. And even if you are trying to trip me up, this has nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't force you to write your statement.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the statements were the ones I gave two years ago. They are not relevant now. Quite a lot of errors were made in that statement, and you're trying to compromise me by bringing that up. And wait a minute. It is I who am speaking now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You compromise yourself.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's time for a moment to cool now. Now, Mr. Samardzic, the accused is entitled to ask you questions about your statement. We hear your responses about it. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that Branko Kostic was a Greater Serbian nationalist. Was he elected under my influence, Mr. Samardzic, or was it you in Montenegro who elected him?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not one of those who elected him, you can be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. When I say "you," I mean the citizens of Montenegro, democratic institutions, the parliament that elected him. I certainly don't think that you are the person who elected him or did he care about that. Was he freely elected in Montenegro by the Assembly of Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which position are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am referring to his position in the Presidency of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is the Assembly of Montenegro that nominated him instead of Bucin. That is true. But that does not mean that because he was nominated by the Assembly of Montenegro that he is not a nationalist, an ultranationalist, as I have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Samardzic. You said that in Montenegro, paramilitary units were organised and that that can be seen. You said that into that same microphone there. That can be seen in the order issued by the two Bulatovics. It so happened that the president of Montenegro and the Minister of the Interior shared the same last name; Bulatovic. This is an exhibit that you presented here. So now I'm asking you: Where can that be seen in that particular exhibit, especially as concerns the order to carry out mobilisation of the special unit of the police? I'm quoting what it says here: "As strong as a reinforced infantry company. Only in the war conflict on the border between the Republic of Montenegro and the Republic of Croatia..." That's what Momir Bulatovic signed. And now you say that, on the basis of this, one can see that a paramilitary formation was established. There is this one company of policemen at the border. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop this. The accused is referring to Exhibit 338, tabs 2 and 3. Mr. Samardzic, do you remember the documents to which the accused is referring or would you like to see copies of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't want to look at that document. I've already seen it. Mr. Milosevic is tricking me. He said that I presented this to the Court. That is not true. I did not present this document to the Court, or the other one either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: To be fair to him, he's not tricking you. The document was presented during your evidence, and he is entitled to ask you some questions about it. Can you help us at all about what is described as these mobilisation orders or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honour, I don't know how this was interpreted to you, but he said that I presented this to the Court. Again, I'm saying I'm not the one who presented this. This was presented to me in court so that I could see it. And now in response to your question, I would like to say the following: It is clear from the documents I saw here that both Bulatovics issued an order to establish special units. To be precise, from the police force and from the Territorial Defence. To the best of my understanding, these units are not purely military units. They are similar to military units, so that's why they're called paramilitary units. At least, that's the way I understand it. And they were placed under the command of the Yugoslav army that was then engaged in war. And that's all. I don't see anything controversial about this. I don't see why I should be tricked in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're not being tricked. You're not being tricked. You are simply being asked a question about the document, and you have now explained. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Again you said here, Mr. Samardzic, paramilitaries, Territorial Defence, et cetera. In this order, show me any mention of anything except a company of the police that is supposed to guard the border between Montenegro and Croatia, where conflicts had broken out. Is any other unit referred to, or any other mobilisation in these two orders? One is a general order issued by the president of the Republic, and the other one that spells it out in more concrete terms, because it's the minister, because he says between such-and-such and such-and-such hours --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the time, it was too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see anything except for this one unit of one company of the police force? I'm asking you about this order. And you say it is obvious that paramilitary units are being established.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Didn't Bulatovic issue an order on general mobilisation, not to mobilise one company only?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about that one and the other one. Where is this other order that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the general order that was signed by Bulatovic and that they presented to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where is this order?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give it to me and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I haven't got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic -- Mr. Milosevic, you have one final question, because your time is up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wanted to ask him about these few documents that he interpreted in a freakish way, but unfortunately, you won't let me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, do you know the Serbian saying that people who lie have short legs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You needn't bother to answer that. Mr. Kay, have you any questions, or Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is the first time that I'm asking you this. I am really going to try to finish by 11.00 with my questions, but if I do not finish, perhaps could you give me just a few minutes more, if possible? If it is not possible, I'll really try to finish by 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you try and finish, because we need to hear another witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Samardzic, could you please just give me yes or no answers, because these are very well-known things that I'm going to ask you about. Were you born in 1935? That's not being contested, right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that in 1990 you were 55 years old and at that time more than half of the population of Yugoslavia was that age?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that what happened in the First World War is something that everybody had actually lived through; it was not only history?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The First World War?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, no the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I experienced it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And at that time, were there very many people who had lived both through the First and Second World Wars?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, there were still people alive who had lived through the First World War too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm actually interested in a few things that happened between 1950 -- or rather, in 1945 and 1953, because you mentioned that at that time your father was in deep trouble. And in 1953, you were 18 years old; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me why your father was in prison? Because you said this in your written statement, that between 1948 and 1953, he was in prison. So for five years. He must have done something really terrible.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that he was in 'til 1953, and it was until 1952. And he didn't do a thing. He was tricked. He was set up. He was a member of the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Montenegro. He was a holder of the 1941 Partizan memorial medal. He was supposed to get the highest decoration, to be declared a national hero of Yugoslavia; however, it was the state security service that had set him up and detained him in Goli Otok. And he was quite innocent, quite innocent. And this is obvious from documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that he got into trouble during Com Inform only because of his opinion?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did get in trouble during the Com Inform times, yes, but his opinion was correct. He was not in favour of Stalin. He was not. He was in favour of the line carried by his party then. But Sava Joksimovic, chief of police in Montenegro, set him up and that is why he was detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Why are you so upset? I'm just asking you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not being upset, but it is really hard. I'm talking about the memory of my father, who was an innocent man and who suffered, and you are setting up these traps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I am not setting up traps.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why is the fate of my father important for this trial?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question is really this: How is this assisting the Trial Chamber? Clearly it's an important matter for the witness, but is it -- I don't at the moment see the relevance of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will see this very soon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to say, Mr. Samardzic, that your father got into trouble --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you would explain what the relevance is so we can understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance of this question lies in the following: In that year -- during those years, rather, about 50.000 people were imprisoned. Out of these 50.000 people, the majority were Serbs and Montenegrins, and they were all imprisoned in gaols on small islands. And this was because, again, this idea of a Greater Serbia was being bandied about. So it was 16.000 people who were imprisoned in these islands, including his father. And they suffered only because they were Serbs and Montenegrins and because they thought that there was a certain opinion that was right. But they were not declared guilty by a court of law. No judgement was passed against them. And that is the core of the matter. And then you can see some well-known things that happened in the aftermath. So I'm really asking you to let me explain this, because it is highly relevant, and you will see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will see, but meanwhile, you've put the matter, and the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is this the way things were, the way I put it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The figures on the number of prisoners could be right. There were far more than 16.000. That's right, but I totally disagree with you that they were detained because of this idea of a Greater Serbia. The veterans of Sutjeska and Neretva who were detained in Goli Otok were not fighting for a Greater Serbia but for the brotherhood of the people of Yugoslavia, of the Slovenians, Croats, and everybody else, so don't try to plant this on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We're going to get to that. But you said in your statement that Aleksandar Rankovic, Tito's Minister of the Interior, shamelessly promoted the Serbian cause in Montenegro. He cleansed those who were not militarily prepared to accept Serb domination. Is that what you said in your statement, that this was a pogrom and that Com Inform was, inter alia, a pogrom for that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Common form was a pogrom against the Montenegrin nation, because you did not give the exact number of detainees. You should separate the Serb detainees from the Montenegrin detainees. 80 per cent of the detainees, the prisoners in Goli Otok, were from Montenegro, and Montenegro has only 1.6 per cent of Yugoslavia's population. Let me repeat this, Your Honour. Let me try to repeat it slowly: 90 per cent of the people who were imprisoned then in Yugoslavia were not in favour of Stalin. They were innocent, and they were imprisoned. Out of the 20 or so thousand who were in Goli Otok, who were imprisoned there, 80 per cent were Montenegrin, whereas Montenegro accounts only for 1.6 per cent of Yugoslavia's total population. The chief of police was from Serbia, Rankovic, and he was trying to take this out against the Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where was your father in prison? In Rab or Goli Otok?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Goli Otok.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where is Goli Otok?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that Goli Otok is in Croatia, but the power of Rankovic was the same in Montenegro and in Croatia. Then the situation was not the same as it is today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is quite sufficient, Mr. Samardzic. I have other things to deal with as well. Is it correct that immediately after the end of the Second World War -- you talked yesterday about the civil war that lasted until 1945, and you remember that. And is it correct that immediately after the end of the Second World War, tens of thousands of persons were killed, either because they were rich or they belonged to some political parties before the war that advocated parliamentary democracy, that were prominent persons, artists, and that this primarily took place in Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the way you're putting it. Perhaps there were a few killings. That's probable. But that this was general practice to kill rich people after the war, and prominent people, that simply is not true. Allow me to say this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I must protest. The amici are supposed to be doing a service to the Court and then they ask for an excess of time when we are extremely limited as to time. There must come a limit to the amount --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I agree. We will discuss the matter on the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we are having great difficulty in determining the relevance of the questions that you are asking. Will you explain the relevance. And in any event, I think we'd like you to direct your cross-examination to matters that are more up-to-date and leave the historical matters aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Robinson, I highly appreciate your remarks, but you know that from day one we have been dealing with the problem of Greater Serbia because of the indictment, and all three indictments are brought together by that. Now I have perhaps come to the point. Everything that I've been asking the witness is directed at showing that this idea that a Greater Serbia should exist has been propounded for the past 50 years or so, and this is contained in the statement of this witness, so that you would see that at all difficult points in time throughout history over the past 50 years, from 1945 onwards, it is always the question of a Greater Serbia that was raised time and again, that this Greater Serbia could jeopardise other nations. During this trial -- I don't know how long I'll be dealing with this case any more, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... have been around for some time; is that it? We'll proceed, but I think you'll have to finish by 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, very briefly, what is the point?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that what Mr. Tapuskovic was saying was completely misunderstood. It is not the idea of a Greater Serbia, but these are accusations concerning an alleged idea to set up a Greater Serbia. A Greater Serbia is a -- is something that was concocted by Austro-Hungary two centuries ago, never by Serbia, and I explained that very well. So this was a pogrom of the Serbs really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let Mr. Tapuskovic conduct his own examination. Yes, now, Mr. Tapuskovic, you've got until 11.00, so perhaps you would just deal with the matters in that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I'm going to hurry up. But I think it would be useful for you, at any rate. But all right. Of course I'm going to act upon your instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, you said yesterday that this idea of a Greater Serbia was created only in the late 1980s and that the creators of this idea were the memoranda, Dobrica Cosic, and then Slobodan Milosevic. That's what you said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that was the leader. I never said it was the beginning. The beginning was at the time of Garasanin, of Ilija Garasanin. The idea of a Greater Serbia has been in existence since the times of Ilija Garasanin. It was not invented by Austro-Hungary but by this Serbian minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. Please, Your Honours, I would like to draw your attention to page 8 of the Serbian version, or rather, page 9, last paragraph, of the English version, where it says that Mr. Samardzic stated, after the first sentence: "... particularly in the north-east of the Republic, they always supported the idea of a Greater Serbia ... After the war, Aleksandar Rankovic, Tito's Minister of the Interior, shamelessly promoted the Serb cause in Montenegro. After World War II, he purged many people in Montenegro who were not willing to totally endorse Serb domination. Many people who had fought with the Partizans were imprisoned as Stalinists, royalists, fascists, or just plain nationalists. He replaced them with persons who subscribed to his view of Serbian primacy." So that was the idea that always existed amongst the Montenegrins. That's what you say, this idea of a Greater Serbia. And then Serbian supremacy, in the actions of Aleksandar Rankovic, as you had put it. Is it the way you put it here, that Greater Serbia was being referred to even then?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, something that was always being ascribed to the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Montenegro, after 1948, propaganda began for Greater Serbism, and that is true, in schools, and it exists to the present day as well. So everything from the educational system; schools, cadres, policy - I mention this - everything was implemented in this way to make Montenegro just a part of a Greater Serbia or close to a Greater Serbia. That was what was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Samardzic. So in 1965, was Rankovic arrested, along with lots of other people, for that same alleged existence of the idea of Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was replaced at that time because of the idea of a Greater Serbia. That is true. But none of his policemen were arrested with him. A portion of them were just pensioned off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The constitution of 1974 -- and in 1974 you were a member of parliament, of the federal parliament, a deputy there, and you know everything connected to how the constitution was enacted, what happened up until 1974 and afterwards. Now, the 1974 constitution, was it passed precisely because of this fear of a Greater Serbia, and was not that 1974 constitution a preparation in fact for all the subsequent republics that were later set up, the six republics and two autonomous provinces for the economic and political breaking off of these republics and provinces?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot define the 1970 [as interpreted] constitution in that way. The constitution did, without doubt, have as its intentions to clip Greater Serbia and the idea about that, but the constitution did not provide for the possibility of secession.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, was there a special provision in the constitution with respect total national defence, that all the people should be armed? Now, who did Yugoslavia have to defend itself from when there was peace in Europe? There was no intimation of war at all.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Yugoslavia had to have an army of its own and its organised system of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree there with you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But after that, the danger always lurked of an attack from the Soviet Union and its bloc.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But why should we arm the people? To defend our borders, that's okay, but why did we arm the people?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if Yugoslavia were to be attacked, were to have been attacked at that time by the Soviet bloc, for instance, the sole defence was what we referred to as total peoples defence, and that is in the traditions of our peoples, that along with the army, all military-able men could also assist in the defence of the country. That was nothing bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if this constitution provided for secession, does any -- let me ask you: Does any constitution in any other country allow for separation up until a secession even?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tito's Yugoslavia had five constitutions, if I may be allowed to state. From the first to the last, they all contained the provision on the right of peoples to self-determination, and I see nothing bad if peoples in a federal state enjoyed the right to step down and separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But this constitutional provision, did it not come into force when Slovenia took the action it did?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When it attacked the army.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, you're talking about 1990 and 1991; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to go into Slovenia did. There was a conflict created there. But you can't blame the provision of the 1974 constitution for that. The provision did exist. That is exact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When the 1974 constitution was adopted and passed, was there mention made of autonomy for Serbs in Croatia? Was there any mention of that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that idea always did exist that the Serbs ought to be given their autonomy in Croatia. I can't speak about 1974, but there were always advocates of this. During World War II, Mosa Pijade asked Tito that Serbs in Croatia be given autonomy. And what did Tito say? He didn't allow it. He didn't permit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you say that Mosa Pijade told Tito that and Tito answered that there can be no question of autonomy for that portion of Croatia. That was Tito's answer to Mosa Pijade. Is that true? Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That took place at Mount Glamoc. I think they met there, and Mosa Pijade did advocate this idea. Tito, on the other hand, considered that there was no need for autonomy because he was an advocate of setting up a state of nations living under the spirit of brotherhood and equality. And at this point in time, don't ask me whether I agree with Mosa Pijade or whether I agree with Tito. That event did come to pass, and I don't know what your conclusions are.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see that my time is up. May I be allowed to ask some more questions, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can ask until 5 past. We'll sit until 5 past to allow you to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I will be as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at the 1974 constitution. It enabled complete autonomy, even including the right to secession.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the same in 1946, Mr. Tapuskovic. That was the 1946 constitution too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know. Now, tell me: Did the right of veto exist before 1974?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The veto was not in force in 1974 in all areas either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could Serbia have tried to have a law passed at federal level, for example, if Vojvodina did not -- the people of Vojvodina did not live within Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends what law you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were in the Federal Assembly in 1978. Was there a complete paralysis in the work of the federal organs? Nothing could be done at federal level; wasn't that true? There was complete paralysis.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't complete paralysis. There were very serious difficulties, yes, there were, but it was not a completely paralysed system.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, had the Serbs been given autonomy in Vojvodina, in Serbia, and not Serbs in Croatia, how do you explain this?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explain this by saying that the autonomy of Vojvodina and the autonomy of Kosovo was not allowed in 1974, but 1945, and the decisions made at the second session of the anti-fascist council, known as Avnoj.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Why was this not given in 1945?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honours. That is my temperament, my natural temperament. I tend to flare up. So I do agree that I am going a little too fast, but it's in my nature, and I don't seem to be able to do otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Try and curb it, if you would. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me answer you straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So Tito didn't permit this in 1945; he didn't allow the Serbs to have autonomy in Croatia in 1945. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But Lord Carrington proposed that Serbs be given the greatest possible degree of autonomy, and Milosevic refuted it. That is also true. And then, when they were going to be accorded this, Slobodan Milosevic threw this chance away. If we in Yugoslavia were not able to settle this matter - and I permit that we could have been criticised - that if Lord Carrington, a British aristocrat, was willing to give the Serbs complete autonomy, or a large measure of autonomy, in Croatia, why did Mr. Milosevic throw that chance away?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you must interrupt very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my speech, which we have in its entirety here, I make mention of the facts that Mr. Samardzic is bringing up now, and what I said was quite contrary to what he is claiming now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You will have the chance to read the speech, and you can make any point about it, but now Mr. Tapuskovic is examining. Let him finish and don't interrupt. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to skip over quite a number of matters here, but you were in Australia; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you were in contact with emigres there, Serb emigres and Croat emigres, and we heard from you that they talked about the fact that Croatia would gain independence very soon.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A large number of emigres from Croatia, a certain number of them, did have their organisations and did advocate an independent Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what you heard two years after Tito's death, and you heard it in Australia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They advocated an independent Croatia. These Croatian emigrants, not all of them, but certain emigres did come out in favour of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement here, you said -- and I think that it would be in order, because brotherhood and unity was forged. We were all equal. But in your statement, you differentiated and said that the Croats were closer to the Montenegrins than the Serbs were.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did write that. Where did I write that? Let me ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll find it for you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember having said that. I was brought up along those lines in that way, and I think that is quite true. The Montenegrins are very close to both the Serbs and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What does "Serbisation" mean? Did anybody try to make you change your ethnic affiliation?
