utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not me personally, but this trend did exist, that a certain number of Montenegrins say they're Serbs and not Montenegrins. That is something that is quite prevalent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't want to abuse your patience. Your Honours, I do not wish to abuse your patience, as I said, but rest assured that I had a lot of other things that would have been of great assistance to you in having an overview of all these questions. But I thank you for the time that you have accorded me and I will end there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we adjourn, can I raise one administrative matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you have re-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. We have identified, in light of the cross-examination, some further transcripts of sessions of the parliament. Now, you can see them. They're very substantial in size and they're all in Cyrillic. I suspect they're documents that the accused has already had access to in one form or another, but it occurs to me, before the decision is made to release the witness, that we probably should disclose them, whether under Rule 68 or otherwise. And I can tell the accused, in case he's interested, that there are I think about five or six pages that we've identified as having contributions from this witness recorded in the stenographic notes. And I'll just read out those pages so that he can write them down if he wants to and I'll make them available to him now before the break, and if anything arises we can deal with it after the break. The page numbers for the accused to write down, if he wants to, if he hasn't had them already from another source, are: 101, 102, 104, 147, 149, 193 to 196. I'll make a copy available to Mr. Tapuskovic as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We need to finish this witness as rapidly as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And one other thing: When we sit again, I would ask for a short private session, again on administrative matters, but I think important that I deal with it at that stage and before I re-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, three short matters, the first one different from the other two in the sense that it's something that arose from the cross-examination. As the Chamber knows, I am conducting this case with the absolute minimum of intervention. I hope that's what the Chamber wants. But -- and also I pursue a policy of never putting the Chamber in a position where it would have to agree with something without having a chance to consider it, as it were, in advance. But we have to say that the closing question of the accused hit, in our judgement, depths of bad taste, given the physical condition of this man, this witness. And bearing in mind that that observation by the accused is frequently understood, as I understand it, as a threat, it reached depths of bad taste, on which we would invite the Chamber to make public comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I recollect it now. It was vulgar abuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It causes enormous upset to native speakers and to those from the region who know exactly what is afoot, because it's both, of course, extraordinarily offensive to a man who's lost --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why don't you make this point in open session so everybody can hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are in open session. So you made the point, but not in the presence of the witness, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. I'll repeat it when he comes in. May I have private session for two matters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is coming into court, there were some stenographic notes that I provided before the shortest -- latest short adjournment. They cover the following dates of the Montenegrin Assembly: The 4th, 7th, 17th, 24th, and 25th of October; I think the 23rd of December; the 16th, 17th, maybe the 18th, 21st, and 22nd of January of 1992. They are only in Cyrillic at the moment, and rather than burden the translation department with an enormous additional task, we may return to the Chamber in due course with a request to meet our obligations to translate selectively. May they be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 340.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Your Honour, before I may return to questions of this witness on the substance of the evidence, may I record the condemnation by all on the Prosecution side of the very last question of the accused, which, in our respectful submission, descended to depths of poor taste, and it may be worse, where he used a phrase about legs to a man who is injured -- not injured, suffers in the way that the Chamber knows this man does. It was an astonishing and, in our respectful submission, absolutely inexcusable thing to do. I turn to the re-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I shall make it plain that the Trial Chamber takes no notice of that sort of question, and in its view, was no more than vulgar abuse, and the witness should hear that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, a few more questions. You made one observation, quite recently --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Just be quiet for a moment, Mr. Milosevic. Let Mr. Nice finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You made an observation that Djukanovic stands in opposition to the accused and that you are not going to attack him. You made that observation in relation to certain passages of your statement where you had apparently said things about Djukanovic. Is it your position, as you said then, that you're not going to attack him because he stands in opposition to the accused? Just yes or no, if that will adequately answer the question.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it, but it's not only that. There were also some small errors in that statement that I made two years ago. But the essence is what you asked me about now. I do not wish to attack Milo Djukanovic before this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And again, as a matter of record so that the Chamber can have it on the record, something that it might also have in mind when it looks at the newspaper articles that are being produced: There is indeed an election under way at the moment; is that correct, and is Djukanovic a candidate standing for an independent Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Djukanovic advocates an independent Montenegro. I think that that's the way it is. However, today a new state is being created, Serbia and Montenegro, and in that state, Montenegro is probably going to obtain confederal status.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One passage was put to you from your statement about the anti-Catholic nature of the Dubrovnik offensive. Most of the paragraph, on page 16 of the English version, was put, but I'd like to read you the last sentence, where you spoke of the Serb Orthodox church and its archbishop. And you said in the statement: "They never spoke out for reconciliation or for tolerance, but instead they consistently advocated the most radical course, with absolute disregard for anyone who was not a Serb." Was that your position when you made your statement? Is that your position and view now? And again, if the question is capable of being answered by yes or no, please do so.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbian Orthodox church, especially its representative in Montenegro, acted precisely in that manner, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked a number of questions by the accused about self-determination or about Serbs remaining in one state, matters to that general effect, and whether this was a position that you had yourself adopted and espoused. You remember looking, on the map, at the Karlobag-Virovitica line. Tell us, please, this: Would a composite state, defined by a border along that line, be one where it was just a question of Serbs remaining in one state, or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that line were to be reached, Karlobag-Virovitica, most of the Serbs would, for the most part, be in one state. But in that same state, there would be quite a few Croats and Muslims as well, and the other ethnic groups which make up Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's turn to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Samardzic, you referred as the base of your assertion that the accused was pursuing the idea of Greater Serbia to the accused's speech in which he said that the Serbs should live in one state, as making assertion for the Greater Serbia. However, given that the accused is saying now that the meaning of the one country in saying that the Serbs should live in one country was nothing but the federal Yugoslavia. That being the case, could you draw a distinction between your position, that is, that you still abide by -- you said you still abide by your words that the Serb people in Croatia should remain in Yugoslavia. Then could you draw a distinction between your position and that of Mr. Milosevic, as you understand it now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milosevic advocated a Greater Serbia, not a Federal Yugoslavia, if we exclude his concept of federation between a small Montenegro and a Greater Serbia. As far as the Serb people in Croatia are concerned, his clear-cut stand is that once Yugoslavia does not exist, that they should be in a Greater Serbia. My position in the matter was quite clear: Croatia should remain within its own borders and the Serbs should be given self-government in that territory, as proposed by Lord Carrington. And there's an enormous difference between the two. His candidate for the president of Serbia, Vojvoda "Duke" Seselj, whom, as I say, Mr. Milosevic puts forward as president of Serbia, has, without cessation for the past 12 years right up to the present day, been advocating a Greater Serbia and says very specifically that, "Karlobag is ours and so is the territory up to Virovitica." Recently he made mention of the port of Rijeka which is further to the west, and he said that it should be a Serb port. So that is the understanding that Mr. Milosevic has of a Greater Serbia. And not only him; the whole movement aspires to that. Perhaps he made less frequent mention of Virovitica, et cetera, but his followers, such as Seselj, a case in point, and many others, they strove for a Greater Serbia. Mr. Milosevic, before the crisis became full-fledged, rejected the initiative by the Gligorov and Izetbegovic, the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, this one, and they proposed that Federal Yugoslavia be composed of four republics, if Croatia and Slovenia secede. Milosevic blatantly rejected that initiative of theirs because his intention was other; that of creating a Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused, I think, spoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is now saying that I made less frequent mention of this border, Karlovac-Virovitica-Karlobag, which means that he implies that I mentioned it very rarely. Now, as I never, ever mentioned it, I ask that the witness find any of my statements, private or public, to bear his point out. And when he says that I rejected the Izetbegovic-Gligorov plan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've had your chance to cross-examine, and you can't interrupt continually what anybody else says. And in addition to that, you will have the chance to comment in due course on what the witness has said, and we will hear it. Now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I turn to the meeting of the 1st of October? The Defence produced, but without copies, a newspaper article contained a photograph. Mr. Samardzic, just so that I can understand it -- I don't know what the exhibit number is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll give it an exhibit number, a Defence one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be Defence Exhibit 53.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, as to Defence Exhibit 63 [sic], you had a short time to review it, and to review it in difficult circumstances of being in the witness chair. But first of all, are you shown in the photograph at all?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not shown at all. I can't recognise myself there, nor can I see myself. And I wasn't at any kind of commemorative meeting during those days there. At least I can't remember. No commemoration at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I think the article says -- we'll have a translation, no doubt, in due course, that the ceremony was at the beginning of a meeting, without necessarily specifying the date of the meeting. I think that's what it may say. Were you familiar at all with formal meetings being preceded by short ceremonies of the kind revealed in the photograph, with people standing to attention and in apparent silence?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend any such commemoration. It might have been held -- it could have been held, but not on the 1st of October. It could have been held, if we see what the Pobjeda article says of the 3rd of October, it might have been held on the 2nd of October, but that has nothing to do with my statement and claims that the government session in the presence of the generals was held, in fact, on the 1st of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, sorry to interrupt you; I'd just like to see the exhibit. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Returning to the same issue of the document, can the witness just have another look, or can we lay on the overhead projector, perhaps, the English versions of Exhibit 338, tabs 2 and 3, I think. If we can just lay the English version on the overhead projector, I think, because Mr. Samardzic speaks English. Incidentally, Your Honour, my recollection is from my brief look at the photograph - I'm sorry, cutting through - I think that the photograph doesn't have uniforms in it, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look at the English version, the top of it, please. That's fine. We see that -- a bit further up, actually. Right. We see that it's dated, with a strictly confidential number of 14, the 1st of October. We then see that this is an order pursuant to certain provisions, and we then see that the order is effective on the 2nd of October. And we see that this was the order that contained the reference to performing specific military tasks on the Dubrovnik front. If we then turn, please, to look at Exhibit 3 - and I'll ask you about the exhibits in a second, please. Exhibit 3, again top part. Again we see it's dated the 1st of October, and with a strictly confidential number 01-14/2, pursuant to an order by the president of the Presidency of the Republic. And an order is made by Minister Bulatovic, again relating to the Dubrovnik theatre of war, as it's described on this occasion at the foot of the page, in the translation. Now, the question I want to ask you is this: Can you help us with the sequence of events? Either, one, were these orders made after the meeting you referred to; and two, could they have been made without that meeting having taken place?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Documents of this kind -- and I'm looking at this one for the first time here and now in the courtroom. Documents of this kind could not have been compiled and written during the session itself. Quite obviously, they were compiled after the session, in precise terms, the one held on the 1st of October, the one that I talked about with the presence of the generals, which is when the decision was taken about the war efforts vis-a-vis Croatia. As this was written on the 1st of October, as I can see from the text, it was to have been executed -- that is to say, mobilisation was to take place, not only just one unit, as Mr. Milosevic mentioned, but, to all intents and purposes, general mobilisation, according to what Mr. Bulatovic signed here, and that began on the 2nd of October. The session of the 1st of October was not a commemorative session, it was a working meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you've been shown no other document by the accused or anybody else consistent with the institution of mobilisation, have you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I haven't. I haven't looked at any documents concerning mobilisation. All I can see is what stands before me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you help us with Strugar's approach at this meeting? What was his attitude at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came quite late, but I heard Strugar, who confirmed what Mr. Bulatovic had been saying, that the Ustashas had attacked us and that he confirmed the figure of 30.000 mentioned by Bulatovic, and that it was up to us to defend ourselves. He didn't speak for long. He said more or less what I have just stated. And I cannot recall anything else that he said at present. He said it's up to us to defend ourselves, and that was his position. Otherwise, let me say that I don't know Mr. Strugar personally. That was the first time that I had seen him. And I had a brief conversation with Jokic, and I also testified about that. And that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we turn from this topic generally, and the institution of military action in the area of Dubrovnik, just answer this question, please, yes or no: Have you yourself heard directly, whether on television, radio, or by being present, what passed between President Djukanovic and President Mesic at their first public or publicised meeting in recent years? I think it was in Cavtat, but it may have been in Dubrovnik. Did you -- it was in Cavtat. Did you hear what Djukanovic said to Mesic about the Dubrovnik campaign?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was publicised, stated in public, that President Djukanovic apologised to Croatia for the difficulties that they were having and for the deaths that occurred in Dubrovnik. He apologised in the name of the people of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we may get more detail of that, from one source or another, later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to turn now to the decision taken in the Carrington conference, but before I deal with that, the history of it having been challenged by the accused: Were you aware of any telephone calls being made before the vote was dealt with by Lord Carrington? And if so, between who?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the telephone conversation in Podgorica or somewhere else? In The Hague, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Involving Mr. Bulatovic, if any, of which you are aware, and before the --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During the meeting of the Montenegrin Assembly, from about 7.00 in the evening until 7.00 in the morning - and this was televised by Television Titograd - Momir was mostly in his office and watching on the screen there, the monitor. And he was frequently in communication that evening with Mr. Milosevic. He told me that himself. And for the situation at that time and relations at that time, I considered that to be quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. A number of questions were put to you on this topic, coming from a statement made by Mr. Bulatovic, so it is said. If the video booth would be good enough now, please, to play a short video for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: REPORTER: The Serbs leaders spent the flight home plotting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVIC
utterances.text: [Voiceover] For us, the only favourable version was that Montenegro withdraw its stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Voiceover] And then my telephone began ringing. Important political personages over there asked, Is it possible that you have become a traitor of the Serbian people? The conversation lasted all night. The phone constantly rang. There were even threats. SPEAKER: [Voiceover] Of course, the Montenegrin People's Party called for an extraordinary parliamentary session because Momir Bulatovic wrote this hard declaration. And Momir Bulatovic's signature on that document is considered to be a separatist --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the clip that we've just seen is one of a number of exhibits that will be produced by a later witness, and of course is possibly familiar to the Chamber if it's seen the film "The Death of Yugoslavia." But I'm happy to produce it now as a clip now or to defer its production until the witness produces material generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Better dealt with generally than, I think, in a clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that Mr. Bulatovic you saw on that clip?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. That was Momir Bulatovic personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... then about what happened the night before and the day, in accordance with your experience?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In complete conformity, in complete accordance. He spoke about the telephone calls, the fact that he was called a traitor, and he had to change his standpoint because of the pressures exerted on him that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions and I shall be done. Was the phrase "liberation of Dubrovnik" something that you overheard? You've been challenged about what was happening at Dubrovnik, and I'll come to that in a second, but was the phrase "liberation of Dubrovnik" ever referred to?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I did mention that. That was what was said. Dubrovnik had to be freed, liberated. And that was present in their consciousness, to defend it from the -- to defend ourselves from the Ustashas and then to carry on with the liberation of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember any occasion when this alleged liberation was said to have been completed or imminent?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question and tell me what you mean. How do you mean, completed or imminent?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... in any meeting at which you attended, that Dubrovnik was soon to be liberated? If you can't remember, we'll move on, but if you can, help us.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember for the moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- about this being completed or imminent, but that Dubrovnik would be liberated, that was something that was bandied about, at least in the coastal regions of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've had various things put to you said by you or said to have been said about you by Prevlaka, and we've seen the documentation showing your negotiations with Croatia over Prevlaka. So far as you were concerned, were you pursuing a consistent line in relation to negotiating Prevlaka, both in your private dealings by correspondence with Croatia and in your public statements, or were you for any reason obliged to say slightly different things or much different things in public?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the very beginning, at any kind of discussion about the Prevlaka, I always held the same position and always strove in favour of it; that is to say, we can win the Prevlaka only in negotiations with friendly Croatia and not to go to war with it. And there was no other way for us to obtain Prevlaka from Croatia. The sole way was to negotiate and not to go to war. I said this on television, at the government sessions, in the government; from start to finish, that was what I advocated, and I feel the same way today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, then --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, then, please, Mr. Samardzic, the actual heart of -- core of your evidence and what it's all about, the attack -- or a lot of it is about, and that is the attack on Dubrovnik. The accused has said that he condemned it, that he -- or condemned the shelling of Dubrovnik. When pressed by the Chamber for an explanation, he said something to this effect: That he understood that the army was being attacked because it wanted to limit the action of National Guard Corps. Is that an explanation for the involvement of the army at Dubrovnik that you've heard before?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What he said in The Hague or in Brussels - Mr. Milosevic, I mean - does not correspond, absolutely does not correspond to the truth. He probably said it, but there was fighting over Dubrovnik. The whole army was ready, and its equipment and the reservists of Montenegro attacked Dubrovnik. That's what they were doing. At that time, there were none of the ZNGs or National Guard Corps, as the president of the Serbian government, Zelenovic -- the Prime Minister of the government, Zelenovic, writes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in the meetings of the Montenegrin Assembly, particularly on the 1st of October and subsequent ones, was this explanation or excuse being advanced or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say that it wasn't an Assembly meeting, that one on the 1st of October. It was a government session with the generals I mentioned. And I attended that meeting in part, and the principal issue was that the Croats were attacking us and that it was up to us to defend ourselves. And of course, within that context, the subject of the incidents came up, the incidents perpetrated by the Croatian side along our borders. And there was even a document presented about it. I didn't protest on the occasion, but I wasn't quite sure that that was in order. So what I remember most vividly from that meeting was that we had to defend ourselves against Croatia. That was on the 1st of October. And already the following day it was quite evident that our units had entered into Croatia and that there was no trace of the 30.000 who were attacking Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You explained yesterday that when you were first presented -- not yesterday, the day before, I think. Whenever. That when you were first presented with this explanation of the 30.000 attacking Croatians, you accepted it because it came from the mouths of the generals. Can you just finally tell us roughly when, or precisely when, you first realised that that account was false and that you first started to detach yourself from it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That evening, that is to say, on the 1st of October, in the evening, I said the following: If they have indeed attacked us, then it is up to us to defend ourselves. Because I believed, I had the impression that the generals were there in full battle dress --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that what you were told was not true. We've had the evidence before. Just roughly when you first realised that what you were told was false.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already the following day or days. It wasn't easy for me. It wasn't easy to see that -- I always believed that the army would defend Yugoslavia, and I always remembered it as the army I had remembered when I was a child. So it took a few days for me to become accustomed to this new idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I need.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Samardzic, for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. It's concluded. You're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, can I not put some questions in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You've had your go at cross-examination, and we really must conclude this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but this would pertain to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about the stenographic notes? The ones that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They're going to be exhibited and you can comment on them in due course, once we have them translated. Yes, let's have the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm going to use the time while we're waiting for this witness to come to give a ruling. Mr. Kay, this involves Mr. Wladimiroff, and it's the ruling of the Trial Chamber in relation to his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered this matter very carefully and has concluded that the statements made by Mr. Wladimiroff, even with the explanations accepted, raise serious questions about the appropriateness of his continuing as amicus curiae. The Chamber observes that not only did he comment on parts of the case in respect of which evidence has been given, but that he has also made an assessment of parts in respect of which evidence has not yet been adduced, and that in both instances he appears to have formed a view of the case unfavourable to the accused. Of particular concern is the view expressed that the accused must be convicted of at least some of the charges. The statements, taken as a whole, would, in the Chamber's view, give rise to a reasonable perception of bias on the part of the amicus curiae. Implicit in the concept of an amicus curiae is the trust that the Court reposes in the friend to act fairly in the performance of his duties. In the circumstances, the Chamber cannot be confident that the amicus curiae will discharge his duties, which include bringing to its attention any defences open to the accused, with the required impartiality. Accordingly, the Chamber will instruct the Registrar to revoke Mr. Wladimiroff's appointment as an amicus curiae. This is a decision which the Chamber has arrived at with much regret, since Mr. Wladimiroff has, like the other amici, provided useful assistance to the Court. More detailed reasons will be given in writing. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I imagine the witness is at the door, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps someone could go and have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dejan Anastasijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Anastasijevic, are you by ethnicity a Serb, born in Belgrade in 1962, and did you study at the University of Belgrade, in the department of molecular biology, not graduate; you served in the national service with the JNA between 1980 and 1981; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: All this information is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had you become a journalist and become a war reporter since the early autumn of 1991, first working in Belgrade, I think, for Radio B92, the independent radio station, and then for United Press International? Did you work during the war in Croatia as a journalist for various individuals, including -- bodies, including the CNN, BBC, and the New York Times?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all of that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Since 1993, have you worked for Vreme, the independent Belgrade-based weekly newspaper, and have you been a freelance reporter for Time magazine since 1996?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all of that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you visit and make reports from several battle fronts, including Vukovar, immediately after its fall into the hands of Serb and Yugoslav forces? Have you also been in Eastern Bosnia in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: All of that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, so far as background is concerned, have you recently just returned from spending one academic year, year 2001 to 2002, at Harvard University, on a fellowship for working journalists?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First, then, some observations of your own on the ground. Vukovar, November 1991. When did you first go to Eastern Slovenia in relation to the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: This was a few days, approximately seven days, before the town fell into the hands of the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In order to get there, what formalities did you have to go through?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: It was necessary to get a permit from the information service of the Yugoslav People's Army, as it was then. This permit was obtained in Belgrade and it was valid up to the village of Negoslavci, which is near Vukovar. And over there, at the press service of the JNA, it was necessary to obtain a new permit, which made it possible to get closer to town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That permit being issued by what authority?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: The permit was issued by the information service of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As you went into Vukovar, what, if any, checkpoints did you have to pass through?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: There were several checkpoints that one had to pass through. The first one was at the very administrative border with Croatia, and then, depending on the situation, there were a few checkpoints up to Negoslavci, and then another few between Negoslavci and Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By the time you reached Vukovar, had you heard anything from Serb media, television, and radio about what was happening there?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, there were many news that were broadcast from the area at the time. For the most part, the news indicated that what was going on was that well-trained and armed forces of the so-called ZNGs, that is to say, the Croatian National Guard Corps, were attacking poorly defended Serb villages around Vukovar and that the Serbs, the bare-armed peoples, it was said then, could hardly manage to defend themselves. And the forces of the Yugoslav People's Army that were there were described as forces that were trying to separate the warring parties and that they were there exclusively to oppose the Croatian extremists, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did those reports match with or contrast to what you found when you got to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: The difference was drastic and shocking. First of all, the Serb forces, or rather, the Serb paramilitary units in the region, were excellently armed. Actually, the town was under siege and an offensive was under way in order to capture the town. Also, it was quite obvious that the JNA was not neutral at all. As a matter of fact, that it was giving logistic and materiel support to the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say it wasn't acting in a neutral way, was there potential that you could see for the separation of the two sides, or two sides on the ground? If so, what was the JNA apparently doing when such potential existed?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: The propaganda changed during the conflict. The story of neutrality existed only during the first part of the siege of Vukovar. Later on, it was claimed that this was a clash between the JNA and Croatian extremists. However, practically throughout the siege, and after it, the JNA quite obviously gave active assistance to the units of the so-called Territorial Defence in the area that was held by Serbs around Vukovar; and also it actively assisted the paramilitary units that were sent from Serbia, which primarily consisted of volunteers. They also operated in the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think I'll come back -- or we will come back to paragraph 6 a little later, Your Honour. Let's go to paragraph 7. As you passed through Croatian villages in Eastern Slavonia, did you notice certain things at about this time, particularly in the village of Tovarnik?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember the village of Tovarnik quite clearly, the village that's on the road to Vukovar, and I remember clearly that it struck me then that some houses were damaged or burned and others were intact. Although I knew there was heavy fighting in that village and around that village, I found it strange. How had this happened? However, I realised that all the houses that were intact had inscriptions saying that, "This is a Serb house, do not touch it," or a national symbol which showed that the -- the house was in Serb possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The other houses, how badly were they damaged, typically?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: The other houses were badly damaged. Some of them were obviously damaged by artillery, that is to say, mortar or tank or cannon fire. Other houses looked as if they had been torched intentionally, that is to say that the external walls were practically intact, but inside, everything had burned down, and therefore the roof had fallen as a result of all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Turning from that particular village and its internal composition, were you able to see a difference as between villages that had a predominantly Serb as opposed to Croat composition, generally?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: The difference was quite obvious. The villages that were predominantly Croat were practically levelled to the Croat, at least those houses that did not have any Serb inscriptions on them. But the predominantly Serb villages, like Borovo Selo, for example, were practically intact. I was surprised because of the many reports that came in on the heavy fighting around Borovo Selo - these were broadcast on Serb television - when I first entered Borovo Selo and when I saw that there was hardly any damage there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you got into Vukovar itself, as you went into Vukovar, did you notice anything by way of a change in the comparative presence on the ground of one type of force from another?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What struck me even then was that it looked as if the presence of the Yugoslav People's Army, especially of its active members, was on the decline as we were getting closer to town, that is to say, I and other journalists. There were less and less active members of the army and more and more members of paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I turn to the detail of that, and as we start to familiarise ourselves, as we are going to, with Exhibit 336, the atlas, Vukovar is on page 23 and Borovo is a short distance north, along the banks of the Danube. I'm grateful to Mr. McKeon; Tovarnik, which we've just had referred to, is south and east of Vukovar. The grid references on this atlas aren't particularly easy to follow, but it's south and west of Backa Palanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well, then. Let's turn to the sightings you made of paramilitary groups. To what degree were they apparent on the ground?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: There were very many of them the closer we got to town. And basically, there were three categories of them: One were the reservists of the JNA that, in nominal terms, were supposed to be under the control of the army, but they operated more or less as independent units. And very often they were left to their own resources. And many of them complained to me that no active-duty officers were with them. Then the other category were the members of the Territorial Defence, that is to say, for the most part, people from that area who were ethnic Serbs. And the third category were the so-called volunteers from Serbia. There were many of them, and they were within different groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you able to identify any of the groups by name or by leader?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: It was rather easy to distinguish the reservists because they wore the old uniforms of the Yugoslav People's Army, the woolen uniforms, whereas the volunteers had diverse uniforms and diverse insignia. Many bore the names of various animals, like Tigers, Lions, Panthers. However, the group led by Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, figured most prominently and they could be easily discerned. They were the Tigers belonging to Arkan's guard. And they had special weapons and they were readily discernible, more readily than all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Within Vukovar, you were able to make some observations. Before we come to those, tell us how it was you were to move around, whether it was dangerous for you, what news organisation you were working for on this Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 11448 to 11459. occasion.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was a freelance journalist. For the most part, I worked for B92 and for the weekly Vreme as a freelance reporter. I was mainly in the company of my colleagues, correspondents from abroad. For a while, I was with the CNN crew and then the BBC crew, but there were others as well. This is an answer to the question as to who I worked for then. Can you please repeat the first part of the question for me, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. I wanted to know how it was that it was safe, if it was safe, to move around. You've probably answered it by explaining that you were with a lot of other journalists, but give us your own answer, please.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: The rule is that, in principle, in war zones, journalists should move about in groups, and it is very rare for people to move about on their own. For various reasons, there were still pockets of resistance from the Croatian side. In Vukovar, there were snipers, that is. Also, there was mortar fire, also there were booby traps, and also there were mortar mines that had not exploded along the road. And there were a lot of drunk men with weapons, and that is also a great factor of danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see any crimes being committed? Did you see any evidence consistent with crimes having been committed?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Nobody was killed before my very own eyes. However, I saw, on many occasions, members of the Territorial Defence or volunteers taking someone away for whom they had claimed that he was a prisoner or a member of the Croatian National Guard Corps. They would take such a person behind a house and then a burst of gunfire would be heard. Also I saw many cases of looting. I remember a unit that were carrying caps and other things that they had stolen from a shop selling Fred Perry goods, so they called themselves the Fred Perry unit because they had those caps. I remember that absolutely no one tried to prevent the looting, and it was obvious that the paramilitaries decided rather arbitrarily and at random as to who was a suspect, that is, suspected of being a member of the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any evidence of JNA oversight, by their officers or otherwise, of what was going on?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: During the first three days after the fall of Vukovar, I do not remember having seen a single active-duty officer in town itself. There were only paramilitaries there. They were drunk, they were disorderly, and it looked as if there had been tacit agreement, or at least a tacit decision made by the JNA, that they would leave these three or four days after entering town to them so that they could do whatever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of this, you witnessed a confrontation between a JNA officer and a paramilitary. Tell us about that, please.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was interviewing an active captain of the JNA. I can no longer recall his name. It was about 10.00 in the morning, when a reservist who was obviously very drunk walked up and tried to interrupt our conversation. The captain rather politely asked him to let us talk and to go away, whereas the reservist cocked his automatic rifle, pointed it at the captain, started insulting him and then walked away only a few minutes later. After that, I asked this captain how he could allow that kind of chaos and such a lack of discipline, but he answered me that the JNA did not have enough people under arms around Vukovar and that therefore they were prepared to accept anyone who was prepared to carry a rifle. This is more or less a direct quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were there for several days, as is clear. We only have a very simple map showing the scale of Vukovar and its size before us at the moment. Were you, in those few days, confined to a very small part of Vukovar, a few hundred metres one way or another, or were you able to look over most of the town?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Like other journalists, I could move about rather freely within the perimeter of a few kilometres. Practically all the way up to the line of demarcation with Croatia, or rather, with the Croatian forces. The only constraints were things like minefields and other places that were obviously inaccessible. But practically, there were no restrictions of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it is 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If that's a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I may put the last question that follows on from what I've been preparing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The behaviour that you've described seeing - presence of paramilitaries, absence of JNA, and so on - was that consistent over the whole territory of Vukovar that you can see or was it isolated, patchy? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: The situation that I described practically pertains to the entire broader centre of Vukovar, that is to say, almost the entire town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we can adjourn there. As the court knows, through no disrespect to the Court or certainly to the witness, I can't be here this afternoon, but Mr. McKeon will conclude the examination-in-chief for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now. Mr. Anastasijevic, you've started giving your evidence. Would you remember, in this and any other adjournments there are in it, not to speak about it to anybody until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Could you be back here at half past 2.00, please. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.02 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McKeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sir, during the time that you were in the Vukovar area, did you ever have an opportunity to talk to members of the volunteers or paramilitaries about what they did before they came to the war?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had quite a lot of opportunities to talk to them, and I did talk to many of them, and I asked each of them, as part of procedure, what they did before the war. And I was surprised how many of them said in response that they had worked in the MUP, that is to say, the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia. On the other hand, some of them tried to avoid giving me an answer, which was also indicative. And also I based my opinions of them, about how they looked, that they were actually officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, when you were in the Vukovar area, did you hear stories about Arkan's troops from other paramilitaries and others in the area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall I raise matters here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think implicit in the question: "Did you hear stories about..." probably isn't helpful to the Trial Chamber in relation to considering the evidence in this case. I mean, it is hearsay. We don't know how many stages removed of hearsay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. McKeon, you're able to be a little more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sir, was there pervasive talk among the volunteers that you were encountering about Mr. Arkan and the things that he was engaged in the area?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure it gets any better, if my learned friend will forgive me, as I was trying to work the question out, and I appreciate his difficulty. But really, the Trial Chamber has said on several occasions it's concerned to be focused really on the issues in the case and on evidence that's reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. McKeon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The only thing that we are attempting to show the Court is that at least stories about Mr. Arkan's activities were widespread in the area and that this witness in fact, on a later occasion, shortly after this, had the opportunity to ask Mr. Arkan about those stories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think, I'm afraid, that it assists us. I see we're now going on to the next paragraph, which is 13, and you wanted to raise an objection about that, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I previously notified the Trial Chamber in closed session about this. We all have a summary of this witness's evidence, and we'll note that in paragraph 13, there is mention there that the content of that statement is based on an interview by this witness with a particular person. And then we'll also note in paragraphs 15 to 18 that that is all substantially based again on another interview by this witness with another person involved in events. And these -- there's a further matter from paragraph 19 onwards as well. And it really comes to this: That the Prosecution here is calling a witness who is a journalist who has interviewed people at various times over events that took place. And that in itself is so far removed as evidence in this case that, in our submission, it's not helpful to the Trial Chamber to deal with the more essential parts of its task. You'll notice in paragraph 15 that in fact that was an interview that took place in 1994, and we're dealing here with events in 1991. So three years after the event, he interviews this particular person, who tells him all about, as he says, events that took place some time before. The same criticism can be made in paragraph 19, where you note the dates of the interviews are during 1994 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think 19 isn't going to be led. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. We won't be asking any questions from paragraphs 19 or 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When was the interview with Goran Hadzic conducted?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, my understanding is that that was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: A week after.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Yes, shortly after the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is also, while you're dealing with it, paragraph 21, interview with Seselj. Do you object to that too?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure about 22 to 24. It's not a heading in bold type. I'm not sure -- it looks to me that that reads as a distinct subject rather than newspaper interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What do you say about 21? And what do you say about the general point? We do admit hearsay. We've said it often enough and we've ruled often enough to admit hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We understand that, and that's accepted at this Tribunal, but there are degrees of hearsay that the Trial Chambers find unacceptable, and we've heard several occasions during this trial about newspaper interviews and reports. Now I appreciate we've got the particular journalist who is having the interview, but all he can tell the Trial Chamber is that this man told him this and this man told him that. He won't be able to deal with any of the questions of the accused in cross-examination, which will probably deny the content of what was being said. And then it's simply unhelpful to the Trial Chamber to have this kind of evidence mounting up and not really form any substantial part of the evidence that is required in relation to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you make a distinction between the interview conducted - what is it? - one week after Vukovar fell and the other one conducted some three, four years after?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Obviously, those conducted three, four years after are in a distinct category and the criticism to them is apparent. A newspaper interview one week afterwards with a particular person again falls upon this problem: That questions asked about it, he will only be able to say, "This is what this man told me," when really this Court should be receiving evidence of what this man saw happen. This happened, that happened, rather than, "I was told this and I was told that," which is simply really unhelpful in the task of weighing up evidence and deciding on how useful it is in proving an indictment. It carries with it grave, grave dangers, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, is there anything you want to say about this before we hear from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I've already said -- I've already said that I don't understand at all the sense of testimony by anyone who was not a participant in the actual events, who didn't see something himself personally, and who is merely recounting what others said to him, told him, without any binding factor. Because a newspaper interview is not an examination of any kind. Many speakers wish to represent things the way they want them to appear sometimes, and not even the way they saw them for themselves. And on many occasions -- [In English] That is not with my stuff here. [Interpretation] As I was saying, on many occasions you rejected quotations, for example, even from very prominent world figures, with respect to the events. And now you're bringing a journalist forth to testify, and all he knows and is testifying about is secondhand, tenth hand, 20th hand, et cetera. And on the other hand, he has his own political orientations of the kind that he is in fact working for the OTP, for the Prosecution. So I think that from the aspects of any kind of legal court, testimony of this kind would be completely worthless, and I doubt that for these reasons and the reasons mentioned by Mr. Kay a moment ago, that any legal court would accept the testimony of such a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't accept that he's working for the OTP. It's not the case at all. But we'll bear in mind what you say. Yes, Mr. McKeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think the arguments that counsel has raised are arguments that can be raised against any hearsay, and as the Tribunal has noted, hearsay can be admitted in these proceedings if there are indicia of reliability. In this particular case, this witness, through the course of his work as a journalist, interviewed many people, did many investigations, came upon much information, but we have not chosen to ask him about all of that. We've only picked the -- actually, I think, two areas that we think is most important for this Tribunal to hear. One witness that he might be able to talk about that may be testifying later in these proceedings, we're not going to ask him the questions that we had proposed, and those are in paragraphs 19 and 20. But as for the others, the witness identified in paragraph 13, and also the witness identified in paragraph 21 are identified in the indictment as members of the joint criminal enterprise. These are people, all of these, witnesses that the Prosecution would be unable or unlikely to be able to bring for this Court to hear what they have to say. And this is the only way that we can put before the Court what these witnesses have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. McKeon, would the remoteness in time from the incident in relation to paragraph 15 affect reliability?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would suggest that it wouldn't affect reliability. It's obviously a factor the Court can take into account in weighing the persuasiveness of the testimony, particularly when weighed against whatever other evidence the Tribunal may have before it at the end of the day. But that it shouldn't affect the admissibility of the evidence. The question is whether the evidence is reliable, not whether it is near in time or remote in time. In this particular case, we will be able to adduce from this witness many indicators of reliability on each of these statements, including the manner in which it was taken, the fact that they were conducted in a professional manner by a professional journalist whose job it is to conduct these sorts of interviews and be accurate; the fact that after these interviews were conducted, in some cases articles were published - we have one of the articles relating to the witness identified in paragraph 15 - that after this, there was no comment from the person interviewed that his opinions were misrepresented in the interview in any way. And finally, the experience of this witness as a journalist, that after these interviews were conducted and through his continuing work in journalism, he was able to corroborate things that he was told by these witnesses and gained some confidence in their truthfulness. Also, Your Honour, I would note that in paragraph 21, I expect this witness will say that the things that was told to him by this witness in these interviews are things that he also saw this witness -- this person say on other occasions to other people in other forums. So that it wasn't -- he's not just reporting that this was just told to him in one interview, but it's something that he heard repeated, which would give an indication of its reliability. So I think that the Tribunal does accept hearsay evidence if there are indicia of reliability, and in this case there are those indicators. To the extent that the accused may have issues with that, those can be raised in cross-examination and can go to the weight of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McKeon. We'll consider the position. The legal officer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've considered this objection. There is an important point of principle here. Paragraph 89 -- I'm sorry, Rule 89 permits the Chamber to admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value, but allows the Chamber to exclude evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. The evidence which is proposed to be given is in three parts: Paragraphs 13, 21, and 15 to 18. All of it is hearsay evidence, what various people told this witness. As Mr. McKeon rightly points out, hearsay is admissible in this Tribunal. He also points out the distinction between paragraph 13 and 21, where the people involved are members of the criminal enterprise, as alleged, and therefore not people from whom the Prosecution, it may be assumed, can obtain evidence. And paragraphs 15 to 18, which does not -- which do not involve somebody from the enterprise itself. There is a further distinction in that paragraph 13 involves a conversation, a contemporaneous, virtually, conversation with the events, and therefore more likely to be reliable than the conversation referred to in paragraphs 15 to 18, which was some three years after the events. Although it's right that we do admit hearsay, there are limits on which we'll -- as to which we will admit evidence, and we consider that whereas the evidence in paragraphs 13 to 21, which deals with statements of those involved in the criminal enterprise should be admissible; on the other hand, the statements of another person three years after the event, about which there is or could be other evidence, is not sufficiently probative to be admissible in the particular circumstances of this case. It would be impossible to cross-examine the witness properly about them. So we will admit paragraph 13. We will exclude 15 to 18. We will admit 21. Yes, Mr. McKeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sir, during the time that you were in the Vukovar area, did you have the opportunity to interview Mr. Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have the opportunity of interviewing Mr. Goran Hadzic, as well as several other members of the so-called government of the SAO Baranja, Eastern Slavonia and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, sir, the circumstances around that interview: Where it took place, when it took place, who was present; basically the details of that interview.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: The interview was held several days - I can't remember exactly, five or six days perhaps - after Vukovar having been taken over by the Serb forces, in a village called Dalj, near the town of Vukovar, which is where the government had been established of what was called, or what the government, alleged government, of the autonomous region of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem. And at the head of that government was Mr. Goran Hadzic. And they called in journalists once they had established a government in Dalj to interview them, and that interview was held under those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who else was present during this interview, sir?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: There were quite a few people, ten or fifteen other journalists, in fact. I can't remember from which papers they came, who they were exactly. And also there were several government members present, as I said a moment ago, including the Minister for Tourism.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, sir, during the course of this interview, did Mr. Hadzic make a comment about prisoners who were being held by the JNA? And if so, could you tell us what that comment was.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic responded, talking about the role of the Yugoslav People's Army in the events, and he was very critical towards the Yugoslav People's Army, which he claimed, like many other members of the Territorial Defence of the day, had not done enough in what they termed the defence of the Serb people, that they didn't lend enough support to them. And they insisted especially upon the fact that the JNA did not permit the government to assume control over the prisoners who were allegedly members of the ZNG, the Croatian National Guard Corps. Mr. Goran Hadzic said at the time that the government of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem did have its judicial system and its courts and that those prisoners would be tried for war crimes, and he was sorry that the army would not let him take over these people for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And in the atlas, which is Exhibit 336, the town of Dalj that the witness is referring to appears on page 23, due north of Vukovar, at coordinate -- it looks like it's 45 degrees north, 30 minutes, and about 19 degrees in the other direction, just on the river of the Danube. Your Honour, I'm not sure -- the objection to the questions in this area was actually raised before I was getting into paragraph 12, and I'm not sure if there was a ruling from the Court on whether we could go into those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Without telling us what Mr. Arkan may have said to you or you said to him, at some point did you have a meeting -- a time when you met Mr. Arkan?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, I did meet with Mr. Arkan and members of his guard, at the headquarters in Erdut that they had just established.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Tribunal what those headquarters looked like.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: The headquarters were in a biggish house. I think that before the war there was also a wine distillery there nearby. So there were some offices where they had been put up. And around there were other houses where his soldiers slept. Zeljko Raznjatovic received me and a few other journalists in a meeting room that was in that house. So that was a biggish room, with a big table, and that's where he talked to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when did this take place?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: This happened relatively soon after Vukovar was taken over by the Serb forces, so it was perhaps seven or ten days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you describe how Mr. Arkan was dressed for this meeting, what his clothing looked like, any particular insignia that may have been on that clothing.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Arkan was dressed the same way his other commanding officers were dressed in: Overalls, olive-green/grey. They were quite characteristic. They were different from the usual camouflage uniform that was worn by members of the Yugoslav People's Army or other paramilitary units. Later on, I found out that these uniforms were actually paratrooper's uniforms. He carried an automatic rifle, Heckler and Koch MP-5, with a silencer, and he also had Motorola communications equipment that was rather sophisticated. His right hand was a bit injured. I noticed that as we were shaking hands. And generally speaking, one got the impression that Zeljko Raznjatovic and the members of his guard were much better armed, not only than other volunteer units, but also better than the units belonging to the active force of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Approximately how many other members of Arkan's guard unit did you see when you were at that meeting with Mr. Arkan?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: In honour of the journalists that came then, I know that the troops were lined up, and I remember that there were 150 members of Arkan's unit. I just remembered I forgot to mention the insignia. I didn't respond to that part of the question. They had insignia with a tiger's face depicted on it, and it said "The Serb Volunteers' Guard, The Tigers."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Erdut, which the witness has identified as where this meeting took place, appears on page 23 of the atlas. It's on the -- about in the middle of the page, due east of Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, sir, at some point did you have the opportunity to interview Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, this is a typical example that we don't actually know what this is all about. Questions are being put as to where this happened when the witness encountered Arkan. He explains that this is at the wine distillery. And when? It was ten days later. And what did he look like? Well, this is what he looked like. And was anybody else present? Well, yes, there were I don't know how many of them. Except we don't know what the meeting was all about, what the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can ask him. You can ask him about that if you want. The Prosecution -- just a moment. The Prosecution are entitled to ask questions about what this witness saw and did, and that's what he's given evidence about. Now, what the weight of it is is something we'll have to decide, but if you want to ask about the circumstances, you can. Yes, Mr. McKeon. You were going on to deal with the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did this -- when did you first begin interviewing Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I first had an interview with Mr. Seselj in 1994. I don't remember exactly what the month was. This happened when Mr. Seselj, though in opposition, was liked by the government, but then all of a sudden they came to dislike him. So the big media, like national TV, banned him. And Mr. Seselj then decided to talk to hostile newspapers, including the one that I worked for, and he became far more friendly towards us and he started giving us interviews. So it's approximately the summer of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what was the newspaper that you were working for at the time?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I did then, as I do now, for the Vreme weekly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And before 1994, was Mr. Seselj willing to give interviews to your news magazine?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Mr. Seselj had a very firm view regarding journalists who he called insufficient patriots, traitors, or whatever, enemies of Serbia, and this category practically included all journalists from the media that the regime did not have under its control at the time. He even threatened many of them. However, this position abruptly changed in 1994, when there was a political conflict between Mr. Seselj and the accused. At that point in time, he all of a sudden became far more open to the independent media.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a change in 1994 in the amount of coverage that Mr. Seselj was getting in the non-independent media?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the media that were under direct or indirect state control, Mr. Seselj had a very privileged status from 1991 to 1994. Practically a person couldn't turn on the TV set without seeing him, as opposed to all other opposition leaders who very rarely appeared on national television. However, in 1994, this changed abruptly and Mr. Seselj practically could not appear any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Just so the Tribunal can follow along, at this point we're returning to paragraph 6, which was skipped over earlier in this witness's examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many times were you able to interview Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Five or six times between 1994 and 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did your access to Mr. Seselj for these interviews change again in 1996?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: His accessibility considerably changed at the beginning of 1997, when he was in the government, and then again, the very same moment, he stopped dealing with the journalists, he said that they were traitors, that they would be tried, that all sorts of things would happen to them, and he was making all these references to journalists of the independent media.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you used the phrase "independent media." Could you describe for us what you mean by "the independent media" and what sort of control the accused had over the print and broadcast media in Serbia in 1991 that was not the independent media.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: The question is rather complicated, and I'll try to be as brief as possible. When I say "independent media," I'm referring to media that are not directly or indirectly dependent on a political party or a particular state agency. As for the other media, I mean those who are under direct or indirect state control, like the state television or the national newspapers, like Politika or Vecernje Novosti, or those that were under the control of the party of the accused, meaning that the editors-in-chief and journalists were activists or active members of the ruling party or affiliate parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a situation in March of 1991 when Milorad Vucelic replaced Dusan Mitevic in a high position in the media? And if you do recall that, could you tell us about that and tell us what that shows about the accused's control over the print and broadcast media.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: This is also a broad subject, but again I'll try to deal with it briefly. Dissatisfied by what was then called the media blockade, that is to say, the fact that they could not present their views in the media, the opposition leaders, led by Vuk Draskovic, on the 9th of March, 1991, called people to demonstrate in Belgrade. During these demonstrations, tear gas was used all around against the demonstrators, they were attacked by the police, there was violence, there was general chaos. Two people lost their lives. And tanks of the Yugoslav People's Army were brought out into the streets, and this dispersed the masses. After that, strong pressure was brought to bear by the opposition against Mr. Milosevic's government to replace the Minister of Police and to replace the director of national television. At that time, that was Mr. Dusan Mitevic. The Minister of Police was indeed replaced, Radmilo Bogdanovic and Dusan Mitevic was too, and he was replaced by Milorad Vucelic, a person close to Mr. Milosevic, vice-president of the Socialist Party of Serbia, and - this may also be interesting - at that time he was member of the government of another Serb district, a member of the government of the SAO Herzegovina, which was under the control of Bozidar Vucurevic. It so turned out that after Mr. Vucelic came to this position, the television became even harsher in its attacks against the opposition, and they even more relentlessly pursued the positions supported by Mr. Milosevic and the satellite nationalists like Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'd like to return now to your interviews of Mr. Seselj. That's in paragraph 21 of our summary. Did the things that Mr. Seselj told you in your interviews of him, were those statements consistent with other public statements that you had heard Mr. Seselj make over time?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What Seselj said in his interviews to me highly coincided with what he said to other journalists as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Seselj tell you about his role to the Serbian regime during the early -- or during the late 1991 period to 1992?
