utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj said that in 1991 and 1992 he had a very close relationship with Mr. Jovica Stanisic, who at that time held the duty of head of the state security service of Serbia, practically the secret police, and with Stanisic's co-workers. Their cooperation largely amounted to the following: That Mr. Stanisic and his co-workers, who, according to Mr. Seselj, had a very important role in organising the paramilitary forces in Croatia and in Bosnia and also arming the local Serbs in these republics, they asked Mr. Seselj for volunteers, so Mr. Seselj said that Mr. Stanisic would contact him and ask, for example, 120 volunteers for Vukovar. And then Seselj, through his party machinery, which was very well-developed in Serbia then, he organised the taking in of these volunteers to training centres in Serbia or directly to the front line in Croatia or in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did you publish articles based upon these things that Mr. Seselj told you?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. His assertions were indeed published not only in my paper but also in quite a few of the other media.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And after you printed these things, did Mr. Seselj ever call you up and tell you, "No, no. You got it all wrong. That didn't really happen and that's not what I said"?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: No. At any rate, definitely as far as the relationship between Mr. Seselj and Mr. Stanisic is concerned, there was no reaction from Mr. Seselj, but there was a reaction from Mr. Stanisic to these assertions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what was that reaction?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I said there was absolutely no reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Oh, absolutely no reaction. Sorry. Thank you. In late 1991/mid-1992, did you observe anything in Belgrade yourself that supported what Mr. Seselj was later telling you about what was happening during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you are referring to the volunteers of the Serbian radical party and their going to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you observe any buses or any people signing up or going onto buses to go off to the front lines?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In front of St. Mark's church in Belgrade, which is in the centre of Belgrade and which is where I happen to live, that's where volunteers were assembled every day. That's where buses were waiting for them, and they went either to Bubanj Potok to a training centre near Belgrade, or directly to the front line. Flags were there, and also emblems of the Serbian radical party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did you learn from your interviews of Mr. Seselj what sort of units these men were going to? Were they JNA units or other types of units?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: These were not JNA units. These were other units. These were units of the army of Republika Srpska, in case of Bosnia, because the units of the Territorial Defence - let me explain this - existed in Bosnia only at the very beginning of the war. Later on, they were replaced by the police and army of Republika Srpska. Also there were similar units in Croatia, like the army of the Serb Krajina or the police of the Republic of the Srpska Krajina. However, it is important to point out that Mr. Seselj insisted that he only sent these volunteers to the front line but that he did not exercise any control over them, that they were under the control of the authorities that were in that territory at the time, whose area of responsibility that was. So if it was the army of Republika Srpska, they went there, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to your experiences in Bosnia. Were you present in Bosnia during the Bosnia war?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, to a great deal, and often.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where were you in Bosnia, and at what period of time were you there?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Since the war conflict in Bosnia went on for three years, it is hard to mention all of it. At the beginning of the war, I was in Foca, in Eastern Bosnia, at the time when that town was taken over by the Serb forces. I was around Sarajevo and in Sarajevo itself in June 1992. I was in Tuzla. After the front lines were stabilised in 1992, I was in Republika Srpska very often, from time to time in the area that is nowadays called the Muslim-Croat Federation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, in your time in Bosnia, did you encounter officers or soldiers who worked for the VRS who earlier had been soldiers or officers with the JNA or the VJ?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Almost all officers in the army of Republika Srpska were soldiers of the JNA before they came that. Their supreme commander -- or no, not their supreme commander, but the commander of that army, Ratko Mladic, was a case in point, and then everybody else. Practically all of them were taken over from the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did you learn from your work as a journalist how these officers and soldiers came to be in the VRS in Bosnia rather than in the JNA or the VJ?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: In May 1992, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was proclaimed instead of the until then Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and after the JNA changed its name into the army of Yugoslavia, practically all officers who were ethnic Serbs - and at that time, of course, a vast majority of the officers were ethnic Serbs, because the rest had either fled or were expelled - so all ethnic Serbs who were born either in Croatia or in Bosnia were practically put before a choice; either to be transferred to the army of Republika Srpska or the army of the Republic of Srpska Krajina or to be dismissed from the army altogether. So most career officers, of course, opted for the first possibility and they became members of the army of the Srpska Krajina or the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you learn from these officers that had gone over to the VRS who paid them once they switched over?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: It is generally known that the salaries and the pensions for the army of Republika Srpska, until recently, went through the army of Yugoslavia, and that they were practically paid from the budget of the Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, in addition to payment for the officers, did you also notice whether or not there was any military or logistical support being given to the VRS during military operations in Bosnia by the VJ?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Assistance to the army of Republika Srpska in equipment, ammunition, and manpower was practically a non-stop process. This was obvious in any border town or village along the boundary between Yugoslavia and Republika Srpska. However, during a certain period of time, because of the presence of international monitors, these convoys had to be sent in a more discreet fashion. But according to the claims made by many officers of Republika Srpska, this never stopped, not even after the relations between the accused and Radovan Karadzic became chilled and Republika Srpska was placed under an economic blockade by Yugoslavia. Military transports, though, were excluded from this blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you ever actually see VJ vehicles crossing the borders from Serbia into Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see vehicles with licence plates of the army of Yugoslavia crossing the border many times, and I also saw vehicles with plates of either the army of Republika Srpska or Republika Srpska crossing the border into Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, could you tell the Tribunal what happened in August of 1994 that affected the general ability of people to go back and forth between Bosnia and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: What happened was that there was practically a political conflict between the accused and Radovan Karadzic, the leader of the Bosnian Serbs. The conflict occurred with regard to signing the peace plan that Mr. Milosevic wanted to see signed, but Radovan Karadzic refused to do it. What followed after that were economic sanctions. Economic sanctions were imposed by Yugoslavia against Republika Srpska. What is also quite interesting was that the presence of international monitors was allowed along these borders. However, according to claims made by many officers of the army of Republika Srpska and also officers of the army of Yugoslavia, these economic sanctions did not pertain to the military and their transports. However, as for the people who lived in Republika Srpska, who often bought food supplies and other consumer goods in Serbia, things became very difficult because they could practically not carry a bread loaf across the border, whereas, on the other hand, I personally saw trucks that did not have any military insignia that were crossing the border. However, for ordinary people on both sides of the border, notably in Republika Srpska, it was very difficult indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sir, the translation that we have has you saying that you saw trucks that did not have military insignia crossing the border. Is that what you meant to say, and did you in fact ever see trucks with military insignia crossing the border after August 1994?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not see any vehicles crossing the border that had military insignia, which is quite logical, because after August 1994 there were international monitors. However, I heard from many sources, on both sides of the border, that military transports continued nevertheless, without any problem whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you observe that at the border some trucks would be let over the border and other trucks would be held back?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At any point, sir, did you notice or learn about shelling from the Serbian side of the border into Bosnia, particularly in 1994?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Both in 1992 and in 1994 - April 1994, in fact - the Serb forces launched an offensive on Gorazde, a town in Eastern Bosnia, and I remember very well that at that time, passing by on the Serbian side, that is to say, going along the eastern bank of the Drina River, I noticed artillery positions of the Yugoslav army that were entrenched by the roadway. When I passed by that way, the artillery pieces were quiet, but I heard from many of the locals that they were unable to sleep because the guns would fire throughout the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say "the locals," are you referring to people on the Serbian side of the border or on the Bosnian side of the border?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the people on the Serbian side of the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, what you learned when you were in Bosnia about Serbian police going from Serbia to work in Bosnia during the time of this conflict?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: What I learnt was the following, from many policemen, on both sides of the border: That it was quite customary for policemen from Serbia to go and take up their duties from time to time in the police force in Bosnia, and their shifts would last three or four weeks as a rule. And they would be receiving additional per diems for that. It was also customary that this was a two-way flow of traffic and that police from Republika Srpska would also spend some time assisting the police of Serbia, especially when they had to break down the demonstrators and demonstrations against the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you learn how long these police would go to Bosnia for, for what period of time?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Depending on the situation that prevailed, three to six weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And were these police officers engaged in combat operations when they went to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, they did not engage in combat operations, at least according to what they said; they usually took part in the regular duties of a policeman in order to free the resources for people who took part in the combat operations themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From whom did you learn this about the police working from Serbia in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what happened was when I was travelling through Republika Srpska, I would happen to meet a policeman who quite obviously spoke the Belgrade dialect, and I would ask him where he was from. He would say he was from Belgrade and that he was only there temporarily and that he would be going back home soon. Or perhaps he might have been from some other town in Serbia. This was common knowledge. I didn't really pay much attention or attach any great importance to that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, what you know about the activities of the Red Berets in Bosnia during the war.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: The Red Berets were the colloquial term used to denote the unit which exists today and is called the special purposes unit. And during the war in Bosnia, it was under the control of the state security department of the Republic of Serbia, and this was at the -- at the head of that was Jovica Stanisic throughout the war. This was an elite combat unit and the members operated in practically all the areas where fighting went on in Croatia and Bosnia, these special operation units. And for a long time it was rather mysterious because the only way in which the members were able to differentiate among themselves were the red berets they had and an insignia on their sleeves with a wild animal on it. But there was no -- nothing in writing, in letters. This unit was very well known and people would talk about it, always with quite a bit of fear, even people who were veterans in the field and had had a great deal of experience. Its members were ruthless, and people said that where they appeared, the grass never grew again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you ever actually see any of these Red Berets yourself in the Bosnia area?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not see them with my own eyes, either in Bosnia or in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: If I could, Your Honour, I'd just like to return briefly to a matter that we already covered. I just had a couple of additional questions about paragraph 12, following up on the accused's comment that we hadn't asked information about the purpose of this meeting or what happened at the meeting, what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, this meeting that you had with Arkan in November 1991, what the purpose of this meeting was.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: The late Zeljko Raznjatovic had at that time set up his headquarters in Erdut, and I felt that it was his wish to see -- for journalists to see those headquarters and to see his own unit and to hear what he had to tell them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he give you a tour of the facilities?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, as his headquarters in Erdut, or the training centre, as it was called later on, had just been established, there wasn't much to see, actually, so apart from the unit lined up for review, there wasn't any terrible need to tour the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what was said at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: The late Raznjatovic said quite a lot of things which had to do with current affairs. They seemed rather improbable, such as the fact that the Croatian side had planes of the Tornado type, which allegedly they had been given by Germany, and that it has the state of the art NATO tanks as well. He even said that his men had taken several of those tanks, had seized several of those tanks, and that he would show them to us, but he never did this. He also claimed that his men had toppled several of these Tornado planes, shot them down, but he wasn't able to show them to us either. And he had a lot of criticisms to make with respect to the Yugoslav People's Army. He said that it wasn't sufficiently patriotic and was not being involved enough in the defence of the Serbs. And apart from that, he resolutely denied a question from many journalists, including myself, which related to the stories being bandied about to the effect that his fighters were involved in war crimes. He said that things of that kind were absolutely not true. And that was how the talk went.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you ever see any evidence, either before or after this meeting, that what Mr. Arkan was telling you about tanks and planes being shot down was actually true?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Anastasijevic, do you consider that it is a basic rule of the profession of journalists to be objective and to inform about events objectively?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is an important rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it should also be an important rule that they be honest in doing their job?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you say for yourself that you are unprejudiced and unbiased when you describe the events in our areas, whereas you are testifying against me?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: In all my texts and articles, I always sought to be impartial. How far I was successful in that, I will leave it to the readers to assess.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me now: Are you a member of a society called Povezano Drustvo, Associated Society?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you're talking about, what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, it is a non-governmental organisation, for example, Selba 1999 [phoen], migrations, they were represented before the Hungarian public, if I recall correctly. And I have a list here. You are the only person, the only Yugoslav journalist, as far as I can see, within that project of non-governmental organisations, entitled "Selba 1999" or "Migrations 1999," and this society generally called the Associated Society. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Quite frankly, I just cannot remember that I had any political activities in Hungary, although I passed through Hungary several times. This is the first time that I hear of that society called Povezano Drustvo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you have a look at this list of media, and they say, "We were in." So take a look at this list.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the usher to come up and take this document to show it to you. It can be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at it, please, and then you can respond. Perhaps that's a forgery too. Have a look. Go ahead. Feel free to have look. You can even have a look at it in your own hands before it's placed on the overhead projector. Perhaps you'll find it easier that way.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: This -- the name of this organisation is still unfamiliar to me, this connected society.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now go ahead and take a look at the list of participants, especially the media, and they say they were part of that, and your name is among those on that list. Have you found your name?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How come your name figures there?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I have no explanation for that, although I do recognise on that same list the name of Andrew Purvis, who was the head of the Time department for Central and Eastern Europe, Time magazine. Mr. Purvis is my boss, my immediate boss, in Time magazine. And I also know that it is quite improbable for a magazine of the type that Time is, with Mr. Purvis and all its other employees, that they should engage in any activities of this type. So that it is my assumption that, quite simply, some of the people who at that time were trying to collect some funds and monies for their own projects introduced my name and Mr. Purvis's name on the list, probably wishing to impress the sponsors. But I can say quite definitely that I have never heard of the existence of an organisation with that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you look at that entire list, would you say it was a forgery then, or what?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't say that. I can't make that assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the other participants? Have you heard of them?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I think I recognise another name, that is of Dragan Galic. I don't know anything about him, although the name rings a bell. As to the other names, I can't say I recognise them, not even remotely. I see a Veronique Mistiaen that appears several times. I don't know who that could be. Actually, it means nothing to me. None of this rings a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Anastasijevic. Very well. Now, were you involved in an arrangement of any kind of the Niemann Foundation?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see, a foundation that is called the Niemann Fellowship for Journalists. I assume you mean that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't read it out properly, the way it's spelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would like to see this document that he has placed before the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. You can include it in your documents and exhibits. Niemann. That's right. I read it the way the Germans would read it. But yes, it says US International Fellowship, that's quite right. Niemann is the name. Would you like to take a look at that perhaps?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I have heard of that particular foundation, fellowship, and you can go ahead and ask me your questions in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive a fellowship from the Niemann Foundation?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I was a fellow of the Niemann Foundation. I did have a fellowship from the year 2001 to 2002, as it says in my introduction. The foundation is part of Harvard University.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you were financed by the Niemann Foundation, you received a grant from them to further your education or to become professionally trained and capacitated in the course of one year; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the academic year of 2001/2002. I myself and 24 other journalists from all over the world, we received these grants by that foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you have a look at this list and tell me if that's the list you mean.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher again to show the witness the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the list that you're talking about, just to clarify that particular point?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I understand it, Amnesty International assisted their connections from Germany and other organisations which -- who took part in the financing of Niemann? How was the foundation or fellowship established in the first place?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: This fellowship was founded in 1939 and has been in existence for a long time. It is one of the elite grants or scholarships granted. If you are a recipient of a Niemann grant, it is tantamount to a Pulitzer Prize. I don't know who they collect their resources and funds from, but I know that the founder's name was Alfred Niemann, I believe, in 1939. He left the sum of, I think, $1 million at that time and this serves as the basic capital to fund the organisation. I also know that Harvard University, which is one of the largest in the USA, has several billion dollars to its credit, and I think that the bulk of the resources are obtained from there. Now, which non-governmental organisations and others who have contributed to the fund, I really can't say. That's not my job. The only thing that was interesting for me when I was granted the fellowship is that it was a highly distinguished grant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that, as you say, the people financing it are the same people financing this Tribunal? I mean this institution that calls itself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. That's totally irrelevant. If the usher would like to give that document to the Prosecution. Now, your next question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think, since you are being financed from these sources, and I claim that they are the same forces that finance this illegal court, that one can speak of your impartiality with regard to your giving evidence here and generally speaking with regard to your activities that you are testifying about here and those that you are not testifying about here?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I receive a salary as a journalist on the desk of Vreme. As for Time magazine, I get fees for the articles I write according to the contract I have with that company. Regardless of whether it concerns my texts written for Time or for Vreme, I believe that they observe the highest professional standards, and until now I never had any serious objections to my professionalism except once.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since you're talking about the magazine Vreme, I don't expect you to confirm what I'm going to say now, but do you know that in Serbia, in Yugoslavia, not in any very narrow circles but quite widely, people know very well that this magazine Vreme has throughout been an outpost of the services that worked on the dismemberment of Yugoslavia and that it was involved in the media war against Yugoslavia for all these years, and you, as its journalist, as well?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I really understand this question. Do I know that other circles know ...? I've really lost the thread of the argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that the Vreme news magazine has a reputation for being an outpost of the services that broke up Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I know that Vreme was attacked by your supporters because of its insufficiently patriotic stand, and yes, we have been accused of working for a wide range of enemies of Serbia, starting with Freemasons all the way up to Islamic fundamentalists. These accusations are really nothing new.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm glad you know about that. So you have been working for Vreme, also for Time magazine; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also worked for United Press International; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think you also worked for an American publishing house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about any publishing houses really. I did write -- rather, I edited a book, but I don't really think that that is of any consequence now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Which publishing house was the publisher of this book that you had edited?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: It was published jointly by the Institute for War and Peace Reporting in London - perhaps it's better to give their official name in the original - and Press Now, an organisation that assists freedom of the media, and it is based here in Holland.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the founders are of that organisation, I mean this organisation based in Holland?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who the founders are, because I only communicated with the editor or the coordinator. At any rate, only with Paul Staal, the man who heads this firm. I don't know what the actual organisational set-up is and who established them, but I know that it enjoys a good reputation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you work for at least three institutions, or four. So that's Time magazine, United Press International, these two organisations that gave you work, that is, that asked you to edit a book, then also you received a Niemann fellowship. So when you put all of that together, you consider yourself to be an impartial author as far as the Yugoslav crisis is concerned?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since a short while ago I think you spoke about -- let me just have a look at this. You spoke about your stay in Bosnia. You now mentioned Foca, Sarajevo, Tuzla. After that, you said that you were also in the territory of what is nowadays called the Croat-Muslim Federation. I assume that Tuzla was called the Muslim-Croat Federation or the Croat-Muslim Federation throughout. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: During the war in Bosnia, Tuzla, as far as I'm concerned, was Tuzla. As far as I know, the Croat-Muslim Federation was established as such just before the Dayton Accords, that is to say, in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Is it correct that in the summer of 1992 you were in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: It is correct that I spent one day in Tuzla, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did an incident happen to you then when you were there in Tuzla in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: There were a few incidents involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is this incident that happened to you in Tuzla in summer 1992?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I would really like you to be more specific, if possible, in your question. After this day, I wrote quite a long report about everything that happened, but I don't really want to waste the time of this Court by telling this entire story.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to tell the entire story. Just tell me: What are these incidents that happened to you in Tuzla in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I was travelling, accompanied by a UN convoy that was going from Belgrade to Sarajevo, and we had to stop in Tuzla because there was a problem at the checkpoint. So instead of just passing through the checkpoint, we were practically there all day and all night. The two things I can remember now is that at one point in time I was threatened by members of the BH army, when they realised that they had a Serb, a man from Belgrade, in front of them, but that ended rather quickly. After we exchanged a few words, we could actually communicate quite normally. That is one thing that could be called an incident, perhaps. Another thing was that after the convoy was already getting out of Tuzla, and my vehicle was the last one in the convoy, so that is to say a few gunshots were fired in our direction but they did not hit the vehicle, so that was that. That's what I can remember. I assume that that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How much time did you spend in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, look, I went to Bosnia practically every week. I mean, I really cannot give you the exact number of days I spent in Bosnia during the war. What do you mean, actually?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which is the period that you spent in Bosnia? From when until when, when you say temporarily you went there, once a week or whatever.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes I went there for two or three days, sometimes I went there for two or three weeks. It depended on the assignment, the journalistic assignment I got.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In which period?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war, and after the war, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that you were there from 1992 until 1995, until Dayton; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Permanently? For a week, for two weeks, three weeks, a day or two or three; and how long were the breaks?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not say I was there permanently. This is a very contradictory question. I was there often, in two- -- for two- or three-day periods or two- or three-day weeks. And sometimes there were a few months in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Who did you send this information that you obtained in Bosnia to?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: When I worked for the UPI, the United Press International, I sent them in - and this was until October 1993 - I sent them to UPI. And also at that time from time to time I had my articles published in Vreme, as a journalist, and then I would send them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me quite specifically: Then in Bosnia, did you receive any money from a foreign service?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not ever receive any money from any service, as you call it; either local service, national service, or foreign service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Where do you live now? Yugoslavia or abroad?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I live in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since when have you been living in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I've lived in Belgrade practically all my life, with two interruptions that were a bit longer, the first one was from the 31st of April 1999, until the 20th of September 2000. And the other interruption was from the second half of August 2000 -- I'm sorry, 2001, until June 2002, when I had the Niemann fellowship.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So from April 1999 until June 2000, you lived abroad, practically incessantly, only with short breaks.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not say that it was only with short breaks. Just a minute. What are you trying to say? Oh, yes, now I understand the question. Yes. I'm sorry. After less than a year -- well, during those three years, I spent less than one year in Belgrade. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say in your statement, on page 2, that you were involved in research that had to do with police and intelligence work and that you monitored the situation in Yugoslavia, state security, military security.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was the exact wording, but within my work as a journalist, yes, there was a lot of research that went in that direction, in view of the importance that the secret services and the police, first and foremost, had in the system that you headed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say, and I'm quoting you now, on page 2 of your statement: "This included research on police and intelligence matters and thus kept abreast of events within the Serbian and Yugoslav police forces, the state security and military intelligence agencies, and governmental connections to or support for paramilitary organisations." And so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you followed all these services and you researched them. So tell me: What is the methodology that you applied during your research of the state security, the military, intelligence service?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Interviews, texts that are accessible to the public, so that is to say the usual compiling of information within journalistic research.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, you are giving evidence about everything, about the psychological profile of various persons, about political activities of parties, about my political activity. Then the affairs of state that I conducted and other people who were in government, about the counter-intelligence service, the intelligence service, the state security service. So practically you are covering a wide range of topics. And then I saw in this statement of yours you also testify about war events in Kosovo, Bosnia, Croatia. There is practically not a single field that you have not testified about. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: As a witness here, I answered the questions that were put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, you mean when your written statement was taken and now, as you were here?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, just like I'm answering your questions now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina practically throughout the war, from 1991, as you said a short while ago, until 1995, apart from what you said here during the examination-in-chief, that you were in Vukovar after the events there and the fall of Vukovar, when were you in Croatia? When were you in Kosovo? Since you were in Bosnia all the time, when did you research the work of all these agencies and the political events in Yugoslavia, and so on and so forth? How were you in all these places at the same time?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Until now, I've never managed to be in more than one place at a time, although I would have liked that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is witty, but it's no answer to my question. How come you are testifying about events that were evolving along parallel lines, although you say yourself that you did not manage to be at more than one place at one time?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you give me a more specific question related to more specific events? And I'm going to tell you where I was in specific circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As for specific events, we're going to get to that. But do you allow for the following possibility: That some other journalist, let us assume, say, that some journalist who is just as capable as you consider yourself to be, who followed these events, would some other journalist draw some other conclusions from the events that you followed, or would he or she have to draw the same conclusions?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I could not really say what some other person would have done in my place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to speculate. I'm asking you whether you allow for a different possibility, that some journalist, for example, even a better journalist than you, would have drawn some other conclusions from the events that you are describing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, he's answered that. He can't put himself in somebody else's shoes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2 of your statement, in the last paragraph, you say that I started doing some things in order to consolidate my own power. Why do you use this word "consolidation"? Had I lost power before that and did I try to consolidate it afterwards? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, consolidation means strengthening. I'm not trying to say that you had lost power and that you were trying to regain it now, I was saying that you were trying to consolidate, strengthen, control over political life that you had then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You move on then to say that I was taking away the autonomy of provincial and republican governments in Serbia. How did municipal authorities lose their autonomy, as you had put it?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC
utterances.text: I wish I could see the whole sentence before I answer this question, because I don't know exactly. I gave this statement more than two years ago. I would really like to know what you are specifically referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are going, in fact, to adjourn now. It's 10 past 4.00. Mr. Milosevic, I guess there's more that you want to ask this witness. You can have a further hour when we next convene, which will be next Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you trying to say that you are only giving me one more hour on the next day we meet, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's absolutely right, Mr. Milosevic. Now, Mr. Anastasijevic, would you be back, please, at 9.00 on Tuesday. Thank you. We'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th day of October 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
